## Copies of a model

| Limit | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Textures of `cloneModel` copies | Shared: one GPU texture per device, image and format, freed with its last holder (`p-morph`: 7 textures for 100 copies, not 700). A second model loaded from the same file holds its own images, so it uploads its own textures. |
| Geometry of `cloneModel` copies (2026-11-06) | Shared: vertex and index buffers per device, asset and array, and in the deformation arena one copy of the bind-pose vertices, morph deltas and skin influences per page. Each animated copy still adds 80 B per vertex of deformed output, 64 B per bone and its morph weights, because those are what differ between copies. A second model loaded from the same file packs and uploads its own. |
| GPU morph weights (`@margoengine/animation/morph-gpu`, 2026-11-06) | Not measured for speed yet: the 16 B a frame and one dispatch per page are counted, the frame time is not. `Animation.upload` still loops over each copy to check its weights and bones, so CPU work is smaller per copy, not zero. Time is float32 in the shader: steps of about 0.24 ms after an hour of play. Copies must share one asset. Driven weights ignore `setMorph`, and `primitive.weights` on the CPU does not follow them. Why: The tracks are shared, and reading weights back would stall the frame. What you see: A long-running crowd loses fine timing slowly. CPU code that reads `primitive.weights` sees old values. Escape hatch: Set `player.time` back by whole loops of the clip (exact for copies at `speed` 1; a copy at another speed samples `time * speed`, so it jumps unless the step is whole loops at its speed too). Use `Animation` for a character whose weights you read or set by hand. |
| Animation LOD (`@margoengine/animation/lod`, 2026-11-06) | CPU only, and not measured for speed yet: how many copies update is counted, the frame time is not. Every copy still goes through the GPU deform dispatch each frame, and each still draws. Visibility is a sphere at the model root against the view, with no occlusion. `depth` counts node levels from the scene roots, so its meaning depends on the rig. A tier with a depth does not play `KHR_animation_pointer` channels. Deeper bones hold, so a far character can show a slightly wrong pose until it comes closer. Why: A skipped pose must still draw, and the deformed output is what draws. What you see: A crowd limited by the GPU gains little. A copy far larger than its `radius` can stop updating while part of it shows. Escape hatch: Set `radius` to cover the character. Use `VATCrowd` when the GPU is the limit. |
| Clip editing (`@margoengine/animation/clip-utils`, 2026-11-06) | By method: an eased or cubic segment that a cut passes through becomes straight keys at `fps` (default 60), so it follows the curve only to that step; segments kept whole stay exact. Works on `KeyframeClip`s, not glTF clips. `makeAdditive` leaves property tracks out, and `applyAdditiveClip` poses a `Skeleton` only, without morph weights. Why: An eased curve is defined over its whole segment, so one key cannot carry part of it. What you see: Very fine motion inside a cut curve can flatten between samples. Escape hatch: Pass a higher `fps`. For a glTF clip use an `@margoengine/animator` additive layer. |
| Engine ticks per `cloneModel` copy (2026-11-06) | None when the copy can take its source's static batches, skinned models included, so a crowd no longer costs a tick of every mesh per copy. One when the source moved since baking, has a parent, or had its geometry rewritten: the copy bakes for itself. A copy's world matrices publish with the next tick; a direct `node.matrix` read before it sees the old value. The time saved is not measured yet. |
| Dual quaternion skinning (`@margoengine/animation/dqs`, 2026-11-06) | Per `Animation`, fixed when it is created. `Skin` on raw data, `bakeVAT` and bone-texture crowds stay linear. Stretch blends linearly about the mesh origin, so between bones of different scale the result differs from a linear blend. Each bone costs a polar decomposition on the CPU every frame. Frame time is not measured yet. |
| Bone-texture crowds (`@margoengine/animation/instanced-skin`, 2026-11-06) | One material, opaque, no CPU culling, like `VATCrowd`. Morph targets are frozen at bake time, and bones blend linearly. Two clips a member: more needs another bake. Texture rows cap at 8,192 of 2,048 texels, about 5.5 million bone frames. Each vertex reads up to 96 texels when two clips blend across eight influences (24 for one clip and four). Frame time against `VATCrowd` and `Animation` is not measured yet. |
| Geometry caches (`@margoengine/animation/geometry-cache`, `/point-cache`, 2026-11-06) | PC2 and MDD are read, proved on files Blender's published add-ons wrote; the triangles come from the caller, as neither format holds them. Alembic is not read: the format has no published specification, and Margo is built from specs and papers. 3 to 1,000,000 vertices a chunk, one mesh, one material. The CPU interpolates and writes the whole mesh to the GPU every changed frame, so upload bandwidth is the ceiling: 80 bytes a vertex. Vertices are uncompressed. A seek back on a URL rereads from the start of the file, and a loop rereads it every lap unless it is one chunk: no range requests and no index of chunks. A stream source keeps every chunk it read. No mix across a change of mesh: the last frame holds. Motion vectors, frame time and upload cost are not measured yet. |
| Inertialization (`@margoengine/animator/inertialize`, 2026-11-06) | By method: an offset fades along one line per bone, so speed sideways to the offset is dropped at the switch; the new pose shows from the second frame after the switch. Not a published speed: diagnostic, shared machine, 58 bones, 14.5 to 17.1 us a frame during a fade against 16.5 to 21.5 for a crossfade, and about the same once idle. |
| Sync groups (`@margoengine/animator/sync`, 2026-11-06) | By design: clips are looping cycles, every clip of a marker group has the same markers in the same order, and a state is in one group. A crossfade keeps the old state in phase at the new state's rate. Not measured for speed. |
| Warping (`@margoengine/animator/warping`, 2026-11-06) | By method: travel past `maxTurn` (default 90 degrees) needs a clip for that direction, and a clip cannot play backward, so feet slide on the part of a turn past the limit. Stride scales about the hips on flat ground; it does not follow slopes, for which `addFootPlacement` runs after it. The clip rate changes one frame after the speed does. A pelvis drop past `maxPelvisDrop` leaves the foot short. On real CMU walks a planted foot slides 24 to 50 mm at 0.7 to 3 m/s against 21 mm in the take itself: the take's own slide scales with the stride and the hips' surge is not scaled away. The surge stays on its recorded axis when the hips turn, so a walk 90 degrees off the facing slides 51 mm. A take that curves is warped along the requested straight line, 62 mm on subject 2 at 1.6 m/s. Not measured for speed. |
| Full-body IK (`@margoengine/animator/fbik`, 2026-11-06) | By method: the torso is solved from the animated pose every frame in up to 12 steps, with no memory of the last frame, so a set of targets that needs more steps stops short and says so in `result`. Limbs are three-joint chains; hands, feet and head are the only targets, and a spine joint turns at most `maxBend` from the animated pose. Balance is static (centre of mass over the support hull, about world +Y, from fixed segment shares): it knows nothing of momentum or of the model's real masses. A pinned foot on a limb with no target holds its animated place, so a walking clip keeps its steps. Speed not yet measured. |
| Motion matching (`@margoengine/animator/motion-matching`, 2026-11-06) | By method: the character does what its clips show, so a request with no matching clip plays the nearest row; the weights are defaults made for loops with no start or stop clips, so a real set may want its own. The root is the hips' smoothed ground path about +Y, with a yaw-only character; ground slope is left to foot placement. Scale tracks on the hips' ancestors are read at build but not in the running pose step. Proved on stand-in clips, on Fox.glb's real clips with hand-labelled speeds, and on eight CMU takes (769 rows). A row whose path runs past the end of its take cannot be landed on, so a take has to outlast `trajectory` by a good margin: a 1.1 s run jumps 19 times in 4 s, a 3.5 s walk 4. Foot slide at a jog and a run is not measured. Speed not yet measured on a large table. |
| Runtime mirroring (`@margoengine/animator/mirror`, 2026-11-06) | By method: partners need the same place in the tree on both sides, or `addMirror` refuses them. A rig whose rest pose is not symmetric keeps its own proportions, so the mirrored pose lands that far from an exact reflection. Scale tracks trade between partners as they are. Switching `enabled` is a hard cut. Speed not yet measured. |
| Spline IK (`@margoengine/animator/spline-ik`, 2026-11-06) | By method: bones are chords, so a bend tighter than a bone is cut across, and a chain longer than the curve carries on straight past its end. The curve's frames are rebuilt every frame, and a curve of points is rebuilt too, so a very long chain costs more than one on a fixed `Spline`. `space` needs a uniform scale. Speed not yet measured. |
| Spring bones (`@margoengine/rigging/springs`, 2026-11-06) | Enforced: 256 joints a chain, a joint in one chain only, 8 steps a frame (longer frames slow the swing), jiggle up to 15 Hz. By method: a tail can pass through a collider it crosses within one step, as in the specification; after the push the length hold can leave up to 1 mm of overlap; colliders hold their pose for the frame during a long frame's steps; spheres and capsules only, no planes or inside shapes; a chain has no twist, each bone turns by the shortest arc; strips do not pull on their neighbours, so a skirt of chains can part. 144 Hz differs from 60 Hz by up to 2% of the chain's length. Speed not yet measured. |
| VRM avatars (`@margoengine/rigging/vrm`, 2026-11-06) | Enforced: VRM 1.0 only; VRM 0.x files are refused with a coded error. By method: MToon draws as its glTF fallback, and a colour bind only MToon has is listed in `unsupported` and not shown; `VRMC_node_constraint` is kept on write and does not run; `firstPerson` is data only; colour binds are checked by value, not in a picture. Not proven: no outside VRM tool has read a file `writeVRM` made (stand-in: read back by Margo only). Not measured: speed. |
| Uneven bone scales in IK (`@margoengine/rigging/ik`, `@margoengine/animator`, 2026-11-06) | Enforced: flat and mirrored bones are refused. By method: any positive scale is taken, and an uneven scale stretches the bones under it as they turn, so a chain lands as close as that stretch allows (within 0.14% of its length at 0.9995, 1, 0.9986). A `CCDSolver` keeps one scale per joint, so `addCCDChain` uses the mean of the three, and `setParentMatrix` still takes uniform scales only. |
| Voxel weights (`@margoengine/rigging/voxel-weights`, 2026-11-06) | Enforced: resolution 8 to 512, closing 0 to 8. By method: parts closer than about one voxel join, so a finer grid is what keeps fingers apart, and memory grows with the cube of `resolution` (about 20 bytes a voxel). An open mesh is filled only from a bone inside it, through voxels with surface on four of six directions. A part no bone reaches takes straight-line distances, counted in `unreached`. Authored weights are the yardstick by strongest bone, not by value: the mean row gap to the authored weights is 0.30 to 0.54, as bone heat's is 0.32 to 0.43. Not measured: speed in a quiet run (Seed-san's hair mesh took about 3 s at resolution 64 and 33 s at 128 while other lanes ran). |
| Automatic rig (`@margoengine/rigging/autorig`, 2026-11-06) | Enforced: resolution 32 to 384, closing 0 to 8. By method: one humanoid standing in a T or A pose, arms clear of the body, two separate feet at the lowest point of the mesh, so a figure on a plinth, with its feet joined, or in another pose fails with code `failed` or gets a wrong skeleton. Fingers are not placed; the hand is one bone. Joints go by body proportion along the solid's paths, so a joint sits 2 to 4 percent of the height from where people put it (LIM-282), and more on a body far from adult proportions. A skirt or coat that joins the legs on a figure of over 4.5 heads puts the hips by proportion, not by what the mesh shows. Facing comes from the feet; on feet with no clear front +z is assumed and `facingFound` is false. A figure turned more than two degrees against the grid is voxelized again square on, which costs a second pass; a turned figure's joints still move by up to 0.03 of the height, a voxel or two. Bone rotations are all zero: the pose carries offsets only. Stand-in: the refused box and the README's figure of boxes are written by hand. Run only by hand and not committed, as their licences do not allow it: two more unrigged figures, which gave plausible skeletons with nothing to mark them against. Not run: a rigged mesh drawn on a GPU or opened in another tool. Not measured: speed in a quiet run (0.5 to 3 s a figure without weights while other lanes ran). |
| Corrective shapes (`@margoengine/rigging/correctives`, 2026-11-06) | Enforced: 1 to 64 samples a pose space. By method: `pose` and the joint's rotation are read as rotation vectors from `rest`, so a shape reads up to half a turn from rest and the reading jumps sign past it; a clip's track on a driven target is overwritten. Not proven: no real file with correctives was found, so the proof is a real rig and clip with a stand-in morph target. Not measured: speed. |
| Weight transfer (`@margoengine/rigging/transfer`, 2026-11-06) | By method: the two meshes must be in one pose and space. Either facing passes the angle test, so a layer with its surface parallel to the wrong limb's and inside `maxDistance` takes that limb. The fill is a weighted average, so it blends and never sharpens. A target with nothing of the source around it gets the nearest weights, which can be far from an author's: 41% to 69% agreement on parts of the Twist sample with no surface around them. Not measured: speed in a quiet run. |
| Face tracking (`@margoengine/rigging/face`, 2026-11-06) | By method: morph targets and VRM expressions only, so a jaw or eye moved by a bone is not driven; the VRM presets are a fixed reading of the 52, and no value stands for `relaxed`. A clip's track on a driven target is overwritten. Not proven: no real model named with these shapes was found and no live tracker has been run; the name matching is proven on stand-in targets, the avatar path on a real VRM avatar with frames the test wrote. Not measured: speed. |
| Powered ragdolls (`@margoengine/ragdoll/powered`, 2026-11-06) | By method: joint motors keep a pose and cannot lift a character, so standing needs the `root` spring, which is an outside force. Motors add mass and inertia to small bodies (up to an eighth of the heaviest neighbour, a tenth of the heaviest limb), so a powered ragdoll is a little heavier than a limp one. A joint's torque cap and gains come from the limb's real centre of mass and inertia in the pose motors were added in, so a limb whose mass sits close to its joint gets a soft motor: with the hips pinned, Seed-san's head sags 0.080 rad and stays there, where a rod per body read 0.030, and Knight's holds at 0.000 where a rod per body fell 0.82 rad. A higher `frequency` stiffens it. The default cone clips most clips. Measured on the Rig_Medium walk at 6 Hz: mean 0.1 rad behind the clip, the worst bones (hands, feet) 0.5 rad at peak. Not proven: Rapier 0.21 is the only version run; no timing yet. |
| Partial ragdolls (`Ragdoll.activate(limb)`, 2026-11-06) | By method: a limb is a bone and everything under it, so a hand without its fingers takes a list of parts of `ragdoll.bones` instead. A limb hangs from bodies that reach each frame's pose at that frame's physics step, so it is drawn up to one step behind a fast parent. A bone of the limb under a limp parent that is handed back alone follows its parent's drawn pose a frame late. |
| Getting up (`@margoengine/ragdoll/getup`, 2026-11-06) | By method: two clips, chosen at the root bone only, so a body on its side takes whichever is nearer. `root` is a top-level node. The character turns about the up axis only and the blend covers the rest; a limb far from the clip's pose crosses the body during the blend, with no collision. Not proven on an authored get-up clip: none is in the repository, so the proof plays the rig's Death_A and Death_B backward (stand-in clips, real rig, real physics). |
| Body shapes from the skin (`@margoengine/ragdoll/hulls`, 2026-11-06) | By method: one skin is read, the first that holds the root bone, since skins have separate bind spaces. A bone the skin has no bind pose for keeps its capsule. Vertices shared evenly by bones count for none at the default `minWeight`, so a hull can stop short of a joint. A hull is convex: a bone that carries a concave part overshoots into the hollow. The box lies along the bone, the smallest over 18 turns 5 degrees apart. Measured on Knight.glb, ray silhouette overlap with the mesh over a front and a side view: capsules 0.13, boxes 0.65, hulls 0.93; on Fox.glb, capsules 0.43, hulls 0.78. Thicker shapes reach the floor sooner: with limits the body cannot meet lying down, such as the default quarter-turn cone on a T-posed arm, a limit and a contact fight and the limb keeps moving (hand at about 0.8 m/s after 16 s on Knight.glb, limits held to under 1 rad over). Skipping the limit correction on touching limbs settled it, but let a spine fold 2.3 rad past its limit, so it is not done; give a fitted body limits it can reach (`swing` 2.5 settles under 0.05 m/s). |
| Saved profiles (`@margoengine/ragdoll/profile`, 2026-11-06) | By method: bones bind by node name, so a renamed rig needs its profile edited. Limits are measured from the pose the ragdoll is built in, so a profile fits only that pose; the humanoid preset reads a T or A pose and its hinges and ranges are wrong for any other. One cone per joint is narrower than a real shoulder or hip in some directions and wider in others. Mass shares are one published adult male table, de Leva 1996. A hinge is a knee or an elbow only: spines, shoulders and ankles are cones. Proved on Knight.glb, with Mixamo names only as stand-in names on the same rig. |
| Balance (`@margoengine/ragdoll/balance`, 2026-11-06) | By method: it stands on joint torques alone by default, every one a pair inside the body with the ankle held to what the sole answers; `carry` is an outside force, off unless set. It adds inertia to feet and shins (0.012 of the whole mass times the leg's length squared) brings the character's island to 8 solver passes at the least, and gives a hull foot a flat sole of four corners while it balances. Its torques are forces through the whole step, so a world set above 8 only helps: over 24 roundings at 8, 10 and 16 passes no figure steps late or falls, and no hips drift 0.0020 m. A stance knee takes its torque from the balance with a spring beside it that has no damper and grows with how far the knee is off its bend, full at 0.15 rad, so `motors.setStrength` does not reach it. It stands and steps at the heading it was added at: no turning or walking. Flat ground only, at the height of the feet; no stairs or slopes. `motors.hit` weakens a limb's motor, not the balance torques, which follow the global `strength` only. Measured over 24 hull roundings each at 8 passes: all seven figures settle with no step after the first second, at 0.0006 m/s at most. Worst drift of the hips over five seconds: Knight.glb 0.0009 m, Barbarian 0.0004, Ranger 0.0006, Rogue 0.0010, Mage 0.0003, Seed-san 0.0019, RiggedFigure 0.0005; no foot slides more than 0.0012 m. On 96 other roundings at 8 passes one Seed-san foot slid 0.0020 m and 8 of the 672 figure runs shook a bone over 0.005 m/s; at 10, 16 and 20 passes none did (known-bugs.md, "A standing figure can shake"). Pushes of 1.5 m/s in four directions over 32 roundings on Knight.glb: 125 of 128 pass the push test's reading and none fall; the old assist passed 122 and fell in none, holding about half the weight from outside. The other three are still stepping six seconds after the push and stand still by fourteen. Those 128 pushes at 8 / 10 / 16 passes, failing the reading / falling within four seconds: Knight 3/0, 1/0, 7/0; Rogue 1/0, 4/0, 2/0; Ranger 7/0, 8/0, 8/0; Mage 21/0, 25/0, 13/0; Barbarian 29/9, 36/14, 43/30; RiggedFigure 96/95, 92/88, 96/96; Seed-san 113/108, 121/120, 128/128. Falls in 128 pushes at 8 passes at 0.5 / 1 / 1.5 m/s: Knight, Ranger, Rogue and Mage 0 / 0 / 0, Barbarian 0 / 8 / 9, RiggedFigure 60 / 63 / 95, Seed-san 69 / 93 / 108, so only the first four stay up at 1.5 m/s and RiggedFigure and Seed-san do not reliably take 0.5 (known-bugs.md, "A push throws"). Not measured: speed, including the cost of the added passes. |
| Uneven bone scales in ragdolls (`@margoengine/ragdoll`, 2026-11-06) | Enforced: zero and mirrored bones are refused. By method: any positive scale is taken. Bodies are rigid and sized in world units when the ragdoll is built, so a scale animated afterwards does not resize them. A bone's own uneven scale costs nothing: a fall with a stretched spine matches the same rig built unstretched to under 1 mm. A bone turned under an uneven scale above it is skewed, so the bones drawn below it stretch as it turns, as in IK, while the bodies keep their joint distance; the pose holds exactly where the bone went limp and drifts from its body as it turns away. A hull fitted to a skewed bone takes the scales of the bone's axes and not the skew. Proved on Seed-san's own scales (`hair_E`, 0.9995, 1, 0.9986); scales as large as 0.1, 3, 40 only on a stand-in rig. |
| Swept collision (`@margoengine/kinematics-constraints/swept`, 2026-11-06) | By method: colliders hold still during a check, so a moving obstacle needs its own stepping. The path checked is the shortest arc per bone for a chain, and the shortest arc about the hull's origin for a hull; if your animation plays another path, this one is certified, not yours. A contact is any gap at or below `minClearance` plus `tolerance` (1e-4), and a motion that starts there stops at time 0, so keep `minClearance` below the gap the pose was solved with. A gap of `d` and a speed bound of `s` give a step of `d / s`, so a motion that grazes a surface for a long way takes many steps: past the budget of 4,096 poses it ends `exhausted`, which is not clear; raise `maxSteps` or `tolerance`. |
| Concave obstacles (`@margoengine/kinematics-constraints/sdf`, 2026-11-06) | By method: `SDFVolume` is only as fine as its grid. A wall thinner than a cell may not be in the field at all, and the default margin of one cell's diagonal reads every obstacle that much fatter; a grid must hold the whole obstacle, because past its edge a reading is the distance to the grid. Both volumes take a rotation, one uniform scale and a move, no shear. A crossing segment reads minus its radius and an overlapping hull reads zero or less on a mesh, which ranks poses and is not a depth. Mesh queries prune with a box round the query, so a long diagonal link visits more of the tree than it needs. `/sdf` is the one entry that loads `@margoengine/bvh/inside`, for the sign of a solid mesh. |
| `p-morph` build plus first frame (accepted only for now, open in [known-bugs.md](known-bugs.md#build-plus-first-frame-of-100-morphed-copies-is-still-slower-than-threes-webgl-backend)) | 154 ms, or 125 to 143 with `PBRModel.compile()` (first frame 17), against three's WebGPU 217 and WebGL 54, busy-machine diagnostic. |
| `PBRModel.compile()` | Compiles for the canvas pass under the lights and effects set when it is called. A later change to either, a batched textureless mesh, and any pass other than beauty compile on the draw as before. |

| Engine scene binding (`@margoengine/save/engine`, 2026-11-07) | Enforced: a save is checked whole before anything changes; a plugin in the save and not in the scene needs a `type`; the binding's component names are refused for yours. By method: geometry is written into the save as base64, about 32 bytes a vertex and 5.3 an index before gzip, with no table of named geometry, so a big mesh belongs in a model. A model comes back from its URL, which must still serve the same file: node indices are matched, not names. A node within two float32 steps of its file pose counts as not moved; a node given by a `matrix` in its file is always saved. Rotations go through `setQuaternion`, which normalises again, so a value can move by two float32 steps per level of the tree. A model not loaded from a URL needs `modelURL`. A restore holds the old and new models at once until the swap. Plugins: the default reads only `saveState`, JSON `options` and getter and setter pairs, because public fields cannot be told from private ones at run time, so a field such as `Animation.time` needs `properties`; a plugin with nothing readable is reported to `onSkip` and left out; nothing in the plugin set has `saveState` yet; a plugin is matched by `name`, so one whose name has a running number needs the same name on load or its own loading; `options` apply only when a `type` attaches the plugin. | Save slots (`@margoengine/save/slots`, 2026-11-07) | Enforced: `auto-` ids belong to the ring; a `namespace` holds no `:`. `captureThumbnail` needs `OffscreenCanvas`, and a WebGPU canvas must be taken in the task of its frame. (LIM-413) | By method: a slot is one save file, an optional thumbnail file and a record, so a save with a thumbnail is three writes, and the old slot stands until the third. | That holds where one write of the storage is atomic (`@margoengine/save/slots` adds no checksum, so a torn record shows as `damaged`, and a torn save fails on load). | Safe writes (`@margoengine/save/safe`, 2026-11-07) | Enforced: a write goes only over the copy that is not the newest good one; both copies bad rejects, never gives bad bytes. By method: two copies, so a key takes twice the room; a write is two reads, a write and a read back, each of the whole save. A failed read of the newest copy counts as damage, so the write after it can go over that copy. CRC-32 finds accidents and is no signature: the 802.3 polynomial has Hamming distance 4 up to 91,607 bits (about 11 KB), and 3 at least to 131,072 bits (Koopman, DSN 2002), so on a bigger save every 1 or 2 bit error and every burst of 32 bits is found, and other damage slips past about once in 2^32. Two processes on one key are not coordinated. A key ending in `~a` or `~b` of a plain save reads as a copy. Files (`fileStorage`): a key's file name, escaped, must fit the file system, usually 255 bytes; a kill leaves a `.tmp` file behind, which no call clears; on Windows a save another program has open cannot be replaced, so the write rejects with the old save in place. Stand-in: prefixes, torn and reordered writes are built on a stand-in storage from the paper's crash model. Real: a process killed during writes of real files, 12 times each, on Windows NTFS, macOS APFS and Linux ext4, which also ran the real folder fsync (run by hand on the Mac and on Ubuntu, not in `npm test`). Not proved: power loss, which nothing here has tested, so that the fsync really orders the disk is taken from the system's promise. Not measured: no timed number. | Two copies are kept, and a write goes only over the copy that is not the newest good one. | On Windows a save another program has open cannot be replaced, so the write rejects with the old save in place. | Close the other program that holds the save open and save again. The old save stands until then. |

A delete of a key never read is unconditional. A function policy merges the whole save, in memory, and may run again if the server moves on. A write is a whole save: no partial upload, no resume, no compression of its own. | Adaptive render delay (`@margoengine/net/delay`, 2026-11-07) | Enforced: `quantile` 0.5 to 1, `window` 16 to 65,536 arrivals, delay from `min` to `max` (default 0 to 1 s). By method: the delay covers a share of recent arrivals, so at the default 99% about one snapshot in a hundred lands late and the view holds or extrapolates; the first 8 arrivals keep `initial` as a floor; the smallest transit in the window stands for the link's fixed delay, so a clock drifting against the sender lifts the delay by the drift across the window; a change of delay shows as motion up to 25% slow or 5% fast, as a game has no silence to hide it in; a spike longer than a quarter of the window counts as a new route, and the link is measured afresh. Stand-in: proved on seeded simulated links, not a captured network trace. Not measured: no timed number. | Those are the published methods, with Moon's percentile over a far shorter window than its 10,000 packets, as a game link can change within seconds. | A late snapshot shows as a hold or a short extrapolation. A view that trails by more than `max` jumps forward. | `quantile`, `window`, `margin`, `min`, `max` and the two rates; LIM-373 |
| WebGPU compatibility level (`@margoengine/webgl2-compat/adapter`, 2026-11-05, packages 2026-11-06) | Checked on a forced device (Chromium, RTX A6000, D3D12), not yet on a real OpenGL ES or Direct3D 11 class GPU. Runs: core (same pixels as the full level), pick, device restore, materials `createMesh` and `createInstancedMesh`, `Shadows` (same pixels as the full level, soft shadow on a floor), `VirtualShadows` with `'soft'`, `CulledInstances`, `PostStack` with `Bloom` and `Tonemap`, points with eye-dome lighting (same pixels as the full level). `SurfelPlugin` at 4x refuses with `unsupported`. | The level forbids `textureLoad` of depth texture types, `sample_index` and a plain sampler on a depth texture, two views of one texture in a dispatch, and multisampled `rgba16float` and `r32float`. The adapter rewrites depth textures that are only loaded to float types; `Shadows` and `VirtualShadows` bind their map twice, `SceneTarget` copies depth with a masked draw per sample, eye-dome lighting shades the same way and packs its depth into `rgba8unorm` in a second pass of the same draws, `Bloom` keeps each level in its own texture, and `PostStack` captures 4x in `rg11b10ufloat`. | Accepted difference: that capture has less precision and no alpha, measured at most 2 of 255 from the full level on the Bloom and Tonemap frame, 4,066 of 16,384 bytes differing. | Compute on the WebGL2 compatibility layer | Measured (Edge 156, ANGLE Direct3D 11, NVIDIA RTX A6000, 2026-10-28, [compute.html](../packages/webgl2-compat/test/compute.html) cases and a timing page). Compute entry points that store only their own texel run as fragment draws and those with a bounded number of stores as point draws, on the GPU. The rest (atomics, workgroup memory, barriers, stores in loops of unknown length) run on the CPU in JavaScript: a clustered-binning kernel over 3,456 clusters takes 1.5 ms with 16 lights, 2.8 ms with 64 and 9.4 ms with 256 (37 to 94 million loop iterations a second); a 64-wide workgroup reduction with 7 barriers runs 4.4 million invocations a second (65,536 in 14.9 ms). | WebGL2 has no compute shaders, storage buffers or atomics. | The same results as WebGPU (the layer's compute check compares both on one GPU), slower: GPU-written inputs of a CPU kernel are read back synchronously (counted in the device's `stalls`). Multisampled and external textures cannot be read by CPU-tier kernels (MargoError `unsupported`); cube textures are sampled there as on WebGPU, seamless; CPU kernels compile with `new Function` where the page allows it (CSP `unsafe-eval`) and otherwise run on the interpreter of the next row. A NaN that a CPU-tier kernel stores, bitcasts or packs is written as the one quiet NaN 0x7fc00000 (f16 0x7e00), so its sign and payload are not kept, which WGSL 15.7.2 allows (any value) and which keeps the bytes the same on every engine and on the interpreter. A CPU-tier dispatch stops at its work budget, 100,000,000 invocations plus loop iterations by default (`cpuWorkBudget`), and is reported as a `GPUInternalError` coded `failed` with nothing stored. | Keep per-frame CPU-tier work under the numbers measured here; [webgl2-compat-roadmap.md](webgl2-compat-roadmap.md) lists the tiers. A transform-feedback tier for own-index stores is parked (speed only: those stores already run on the scatter tier with the same pixels, about 0.09 ms more per stored word, measured in the roadmap). |

| Sciviz medical and array formats (`@margoengine/sciviz/formats`, 2026-11-07) | By the readers ([formats.ts](../packages/sciviz/src/formats.ts), [formats.test.js](../packages/sciviz/tests/formats.test.js)): NIfTI datatypes 2, 4, 8, 16, 64, 128, 256, 512, 768, 1024, 1280 and 2304; DICOM uncompressed pixel data of 8, 16 or 32 bits; Zarr regular chunks with the bytes, gzip, zlib, crc32c and transpose codecs. JSON cannot tell `1.0` from `1`, so a Zarr integer fill value written with a fraction part is taken as the integer. | Refused with code `unsupported`, naming what: NIfTI complex and 128-bit types; DICOM compressed transfer syntaxes (JPEG, JPEG-LS, JPEG 2000, RLE), 1-bit pixels, YBR_PARTIAL_422 and 420, odd-width YBR_FULL_422, 32-bit OW pixel data in explicit VR big endian (retired PS3.5 A.3 leaves its word order open), and multi-frame images whose Frame Increment Pointer is not Frame Time or Frame Time Vector (frames that step through space); Zarr blosc, zstd, lz4, sharding, filters, storage transformers and unknown extensions without `must_understand: false`. A file that has both a Modality LUT Sequence and rescale values is a `RangeError` (PS3.3 C.11.1 allows one). A series must share one size and SeriesInstanceUID. The volume draws axis-aligned in index order; `matrix` gives the voxel to world or patient transform for other data. `RangeError` for a damaged file or a box outside the array. | Decode compressed DICOM pixels with your own codec and pass the slices to `dicomSeries` as `DICOMImage` objects; recompress Zarr with gzip or zlib. |
| Sciviz unstructured grids (`@margoengine/sciviz/grids`, 2026-11-08) | Linear tetrahedra (10), hexahedra (12), wedges (13) and pyramids (14); `parseVtk` also reads voxels (11) as hexahedra. One value per point or per cell. | Surface and slice are built on the CPU each call; a moved slice is a new `sliceGrid` call and `layer.update(set)`. Cells are taken as convex with planar faces; a twisted hexahedron face is split along its 0-2 diagonal. | `parseVtk` reads legacy files up to version 4.2 (CELLS with a count before each cell); version 5.1 files (OFFSETS and CONNECTIVITY), XML `.vtu`, binary `long` data and other DATASET kinds are refused naming what. Other cell types (vertices, lines, surface and quadratic cells) are skipped and counted in `skipped`. Wedges follow VTK's corrected order (0-1-2 counter-clockwise seen from 3-4-5); a file written in the older drawn order shows those wedges inside out. | Convert 5.1 or `.vtu` files to legacy 4.2 in ParaView (File, Save Data, legacy VTK), or pass the arrays to the grid functions directly. |
| Sciviz graph layouts (`@margoengine/sciviz/graph`, 2026-11-08) | Any node count the memory holds; edges up to the GPU's `maxStorageBufferBindingSize` / 8 per layer (16,777,216 at the 128 MiB default). | The layout runs on the main thread, one iteration per `step()`, about E + N log N work; `run()` yields between iterations. No speed is claimed. | Undirected straight edges; weights scale the pull. No frame walls (a pull toward the origin instead), no edge-crossing or label placement. Like any force layout it can settle in a local minimum; ten 24-node ring seeds at the default theta 0.9 settle with edges 3 % to 6 % uneven and no crossing. The tree opens cells by Barnes's 1994 test (d > side / theta + the centre of mass's offset), not the 1986 one, which kept one ring seed in ten (seed 3) crossed with edges 13 % uneven: on a 20,000-node graph that opens 10 % more cells on the first step in 2D (19 % in 3D) and 21 % (41 %) over the next 100 steps, counted. The layer frames the positions it was made with unless `bounds` is given. Edges are one-pixel lines. | Run the layout in a worker and send `positions` to `layer.setPositions`; pass `bounds` for a layout that will grow. |
| Sciviz geographic layers (`@margoengine/sciviz/geo`, 2026-11-08) | Zoom 0 to 24; up to `maxTiles` tiles per layer (default 256), all loaded at one zoom when the layer is made. | Each tile is a 16 by 16 grid projected in the vertex shader; a 256-tile layer is 256 draws. | Raster tiles only (PNG, JPEG or anything `createImageBitmap` reads), one zoom per layer, no level-of-detail streaming as the camera moves. Mercator ends at about 85.05 degrees; the globe is the WGS 84 ellipsoid with heights along its normal. A 404 tile counts in `missing` and stays empty; other HTTP errors reject. No vector tiles, no datum shifts. | Make a new layer at a higher zoom for a smaller `area`; use `@margoengine/terrain` for heights from tiles. |
| Light-tier frame rate | Enforced ([index.ts](../packages/quality/src/index.ts)): `paceEngine` holds the light tier to an even rate of at least 60 FPS: 60 on 60, 120 and 240 Hz, 72 on 144 Hz, 83 on 165 Hz, 67 on 200 Hz, and every refresh of 75, 90 and 100 Hz. | Each frame spans a whole number of refreshes, so the rate cannot land on exactly 60 on every display, and an uneven 60 on 100 Hz would judder. | A 100 Hz display renders 100 FPS on the light tier, which asks twice the GPU work of the 50 FPS it used to get; a GPU that cannot keep up misses refreshes as it would on any uncapped tier. Not yet seen on a physical panel at any of these rates: the numbers come from a stand-in clock, a real page on a simulated 100 Hz clock and a fake clock in the unit test. | `capFrameRate(engine, rate)` sets another rate; `?quality=high` is not paced. |
| Supersampled stills (`@margoengine/quality/ssaa`, 2026-11-06) | Enforced ([ssaa.ts](../packages/quality/src/ssaa.ts)): 1 to 1024 frames, picture size up to the device's `maxTextureDimension2D`. Each sample is a full render, so cost grows with `samples`. Two `rgba32float` sums, the frame and image textures and a read buffer live during a still (44 bytes a pixel, 365 MB at 3840 x 2160). The picture is opaque 8-bit display colour: no alpha, no HDR. A size other than the canvas makes effects that size themselves to the frame rebuild their textures, twice per still, and core keeps its 4x target for that size until the next one. History effects soften a still: with `TAA` attached a 16-sample still reads 27 dB against the same still without it. `TAAUpscale` throws, as it does with any view. | Each sample is a full render, so cost grows with `samples`. | With `TAA` attached a 16-sample still reads 27 dB against the same still without it, and `TAAUpscale` throws. | Dispose `TAA` (and any `TAAUpscale`) before the still and attach it again after, and lower `samples` to cut the cost. |
| Feature scaling (`@margoengine/quality/features`, 2026-11-06) | A step that saved under 3% of the frame rests 120 decisions, about a minute at 60 FPS. | A saving is the frame cost before minus after one step, over one 30-frame window: anything else that moves the cost in that window counts toward it, and a measured value is averaged with the last, so it corrects over time. | A step of shadow `resolution` or `cascades` or of the fog `grid` allocates textures, one hitch each. A `VolumetricFog` switched off keeps its grid and its idle pass. The first use of a shadow filter compiles shaders, one hitch per filter. Cutting `camera.far` removes what lies past it. It lowers nothing when every knob is at its floor or resting. | Leave a target out of `featureKnobs` (for example `shadows`) to keep it fixed, or write your own `FeatureKnob` (see `optionKnob`) with a `weight`. Pair a lowered `camera.far` with fog. |
| Battery and heat (`@margoengine/quality/power`, 2026-11-06) | Heat takes about half a minute to show at 60 FPS, longer at lower rates. | Not measured on a machine really throttling: `FrameDrift` is proved on modelled frame costs. Battery status is Chromium only, and CPU pressure is Chromium only and says nothing of the GPU; elsewhere frame times are the only source, so a machine on battery stays at level 0. | A scene that grows heavier gradually, with no step above 15% between readings, reads as heat. A full-tier page keeps its 4x multisampling until its next load. | Call `restart()` on the watch after a change you made, so growth you caused is not read as heat, and raise `rise` if it fires too soon. On the full tier pass `reload: () => location.reload()` to `watchPower` to move to the light tier at once. |
| GPU reading against `FAST_GPU_MS` | Measured (voxel sandbox, seed 1, 1920 x 1000, 2026-11-05): an Apple M6 reads 8.8 ms in Chrome 157 and 8.7 ms in Playwright WebKit 27.2 at 60 FPS, an RTX A6000 4.5 ms in Edge. | The limit is 8 ms, chosen on Plaza from an A6000, an Intel UHD and an Arc 140V. | An M6 sits just over the limit on this scene, so it stays on the light tier at 60 Hz; on a simulated 100 Hz clock it read 5.5 to 7.0 ms and stored the full tier. Only a core `Mesh` can sit below a root. `follow` needs a `kinematicPosition` body on a core `Mesh`, and a mesh that jumps in one step moves its body at the speed that takes, pushing what it meets as hard. | Own physics kernel (`@margoengine/physics/next`, preview, 2026-11-07) | Enforced: 4,194,304 bodies per world, a world per Wasm instance, and 32-bit offsets inside it; `KernelWorld` throws above that or where memory cannot grow. Substeps run from 1 to 65,535. | By method: the integrator's own error against a parabola is `g h t / 2`, so it halves when substeps double; a dynamic body with no mass does not fall, and additional mass is spread as the colliders are, so it scales the inertia with the mass. Shapes today: ball, box, capsule, each with a closed-form mass, and hull. Enforced: a hull is a closed convex polyhedron with flat faces of at most 256 edges and no two neighbours that are one plane split in two, within about 0.8 degrees with every corner within half of FLAT, 1e-4 of the hull's size, of the other's plane (a mesh with such faces loses contact points, Gregorius 2015, so `addHull` refuses it); a real crease under 0.8 degrees between faces too wide to be one flat face is taken, as a hull of random points has them; its rows last for the world's life. By method: the separating axis test is linear in vertices per face and quadratic in edges, with no hill climbing or cached axis yet, so a hull of hundreds of faces costs a step more than it should until the quiet pass. By method: GJK stops after 64 descents, and the expanding polytope holds 96 vertices and 192 faces; a depth search that runs out gives no contact for that step and the next step tries again. By method: a point with a new id continues an old one within 2 cm on the first body, so a contact that jumps further starts its impulses from zero. By method: a contact's normal is found once a step and held for its substeps, and a point the body has not yet reached acts as a plane (Catto 2013's speculative point), so a fast body passing a corner can feel a ghost of that plane; not measured, batch 126 owns it. Contact defaults: 8 substeps, 2 passes, 120 Hz capped at a quarter of the substep rate, damping ratio 10, slop 0.2 mm, push speed 3 m/s. By method (2026-11-08): at one pass a substep a contact between two dynamic bodies that neither dominates is capped at an eighth of the substep rate (30 Hz at 4 substeps) while it carries under 50 times the lighter body's weight, as one pass settles no pile at a quarter; the ground, kinematic and dominant bodies and heavier loads keep the quarter. Measured at 4 substeps of one pass: the 20-row pyramid sleeps at 2.3 s, its top moved 32 mm, its bottom row 1.19 mm into the floor; 30 rows, whose bottom pairs carry about 40 times a cube's weight, sleep at 2.0 s and rest at 5.9e-4 m/s with sleeping off; the 1:100 and 1:1000 stacks keep the quarter and sag 14.4 and 137 mm. A deeper pile whose bottom pairs pass 50 times takes the quarter there; not measured past 30 rows. By method (2026-11-07): a substep relaxes as many times as it pushes, so 2 relaxing passes of joints and contacts at the defaults where there was 1: one pass left the friction anchors' push in a pile of 14 rows or more as speed, and it rocked for good. By method: a manifold's normal rows sweep until no impulse moves by more than rounding, at most 16 sweeps a pass, on the points' speeds alone; a relaxing pass settles in 3 to 8 sweeps on the 1:1000 stack. By method (2026-11-08): a manifold of four points ends each sweep with the exact step along the one pattern of its impulses that moves no body, the points' shares of one load among themselves, which the sweeps settled only by the leak (about 3 percent a sweep), so a soft pass ran all 16; it now settles in about 4 (perf-history 80). Friction keeps one sweep. By method (2026-11-08): inside the slop a biased pass closes a point rigidly to the slop's depth, (gap + slop) / h as a speculative row (Catto's Solver2D soft step), and the soft push acts only past it, so every point of a resting manifold rests at the same depth whatever its load: a cube released on a slope below tan t = mu holds under 1e-6 m from its first second (it moved up to 3.8e-5 m as its points sank at speeds that followed their loads). By method (2026-11-08): a ball or a capsule meets the other surface at its core plus its radius along the normal, wherever it has turned to, so a rolling ball's point stays on the floor; its lever arm stays the step's contact point. By method (2026-11-08): a point struck while its gap is still open notes the speed it will meet the surface with, v^2 = v0^2 + 2 a d over the gap, gravity's gain added, so a ball from 1 m at e 0.5 peaks at 0.2487 m at the defaults and 0.2473 m at 4 substeps of one pass (was 0.2481 and 0.2432). By method: a resting contact sags by its load over its stiffness, which follows the lighter body, so a heavy box on a light one sits deeper: 3.9 mm at 1:100 and 3.5 cm at 1:1000 with metre cubes. By method: the reduction always keeps the deepest point, so its area can fall short of the best four: 0.711 of the best at worst and 0.9915 on average over 3,000 random sets. Enforced: 536,870,912 pair rows and 32-bit offsets inside the block; a step throws when memory cannot hold the pairs. By method: pairs are found once a step over the motion expected at its start, so a body a contact turns round mid-step can leave its fat box until the next step; the margin is 0.04 m at any body size; a fixed body written by hand needs `touch`; a collider's row comes back only after a step. A single add or removal costs one pass over the lists, so adding one collider a frame to a very large world pays for the whole list. Until the narrow phase lands, two bodies touch when their fat boxes overlap, so islands run larger than they will. Writing a sleeper's columns does not wake it. A body at a steady pose with its energy under the threshold can go to sleep mid-air if nothing pushes it, as gravity is not a force the sleep test sees: a body at rest under gravity moves, so this needs zero gravity or `gravityScale` 0. | Own physics joints (`@margoengine/physics/next`, preview, 2026-11-07) | By method: locks are exact along a path of joints, so a chain of 50 hung straight holds a 1000:1 end mass to under 1e-5 of its length, at rest and swung at 3 m/s. Pairs are found once a step, so without it a joint 6 m open jumps a body past a wall in one substep. Cost: a wide gap takes more steps, and on the proof scenes it acted on 5 rows of 6,960 in the limb and moved no figure. (3) Where rows nearly depend on each other a push is a Gauss-Newton step outside its model, so a body's turn may rise by at most 0.2 rad a substep times N / M, and its centre by that much of its arm, N what the path asks and M what its bodies would each move (Buss and Kim 2005, section 4; they use 0.79 rad for inverse kinematics, here 0.79 lets a taut chain reach 39 m/s and 0.1 starts to cut the chain of fifty). A valid scene reaches it when a chain is pulled straight between two points further apart than it is long, the same pose as an arm reaching past its reach. (4) A warm start that would add more than a push's energy, half the island's mass times 3 m/s squared, is taken only as far as the minimum of the quadratic the passes descend. By method: a lock is exact and a contact is a capped spring, so a joint stretched through a wall drags its body through at about 1.5 m/s. By method: a turn past about 1 rad a substep leaves rows nothing to read, so a lock on a hub at 77 rad/s holds with 2 substeps, to 13 m on a radius of 10, and with 1 substep runs away and is refused after 59 steps. By design: a body past 1e15 in position or speed stops the world with `failed`, checked at the end of a step: a run away faster than that within one step would get past it, not seen in 200 random webs of 10,000 steps. | Own physics continuous collision (`@margoengine/physics/next`, preview, 2026-11-08) (LIM-506) | By design: Rapier's `ccd_enabled` as `ccd` on `addBody` and `body.ccd`, and `is_ccd_active` as `body.ccdActive`. After each step a dynamic body with `ccd` that moved further than its thinnest piece is thick is swept from the pose the step began at to the pose it ended at, against every collider whose fat box meets its path's box, and put back to its first touch with its velocity kept; the next step's contacts then stop it. Stopped on a body that moves and runs no sweep of its own (a kinematic body, or a dynamic one without `ccd`), it rides with that body for the rest of the step, and a moving body that comes at it after it stopped carries it the same way. A surface the body already touches at the start of a step holds it no deeper than half its thickness. A slow body, or one with `ccd` off, moves exactly as before (the same bits), and so does a fast one sliding on a floor. Rapier's `min_ccd_dt`, `max_ccd_substeps`, `soft_ccd_prediction` and CCD sensor events are not served yet (batch 140.5). Measured (`tests/next-ccd.test.js`): 1,000 bullets at 300 m/s turning at up to 50 rad/s, as 2 cm balls, boxes and capsules, at a 2 cm box wall, a two-triangle mesh and a height field stood on end: with `ccd` no bullet's centre reaches the wall's middle plane; without it boxes pass; 200 spinning bullets at a 2 cm kinematic wall coming at 20 m/s, and at a free dynamic plate, never end a step past its middle. Rapier 0.21 with `ccd` on, as a black box through the root entry, on the same 1,000 shots: 974 balls, 189 boxes and 2 capsules end a step with their centre past the far face of the 2 cm box wall (they stop at the touch, then the next step carries them into the wall and its contacts push them out on the far side); 4 boxes pass the two-triangle mesh; none pass the height field. By method: conservative advancement (Mirtich 1996, as Catto sets it out in 2013) on a lower bound of the gap from GJK's closest points and support planes. | The sweep tests every collider's fat box against the path's box, with no tree over colliders, so a CCD body costs time in proportion to the colliders in the world; a body is put back to its first touch, so it loses the rest of that step's motion. | Own physics cylinders and cones (`@margoengine/physics/next`, preview, 2026-11-08) (LIM-512) | By design: Rapier's `cylinder`, `cone`, `roundCylinder` and `roundCone` as `cylinder` and `cone` with `radius`, `halfHeight` (along local Y, a cone's apex at +`halfHeight`) and `borderRadius` (default 0), as colliders and as compound parts, with rays, shape casts and point queries on them. | Own physics convex decomposition (`@margoengine/physics/decomposition`, 2026-11-08) (LIM-517) | By design: `convexDecomposition(mesh, options)` returns `{shape: 'convexDecomposition', parts, concavity}`, a collider on `/next` and on the root entry; `/next` refuses the raw mesh with an `unsupported` MargoError naming the entry, so the search is never on its path. The method of Wei, Liu, Ling and Su 2022 (CoACD): concavity max(Hb, 0.3 Rv) on the mesh scaled to a largest side of 1, 3,000 samples per unit area, Monte Carlo tree search over 20 axis planes per axis, 500 iterations, 4 cuts ahead, ternary refinement, merging. | Own physics body kinds and mass (`@margoengine/physics/next`, preview, 2026-11-07) | By method: a body that stops being fixed finds the fixed colliders its boxes overlap by one walk over the sorted ends, so `setType` costs the world's collider count once; a body made fixed drops its pairs with fixed bodies. | Own 2D physics solver (`packages/physics2d/kernel`, native only until `@margoengine/physics2d/next`, 2026-11-08) (LIM-527) | Enforced: polygons of up to 8 corners; by default 4 substeps a step, each one biased and one relaxing pass. | Contacts are soft constraints with substeps (Catto, Solver2D, 2024): springs that push an overlap out at no more than 3 m/s, so stacks do not hop, held to a quarter of the substep rate (60 Hz), or an eighth (30 Hz) for an unloaded pair of dynamic bodies at one pass, which lets a deep pile settle and sleep. | By method: a pile sits lower than its boxes add up to, by its load over the springs: a two-point contact carrying load L sinks L g k / (2 omega^2), k the point's inverse effective mass. The contacts are solved colour by colour, coloured from the top of the scene down along gravity, so a pile rests the same whatever order its bodies were made in. The 100-row pyramid's top drops 684 mm by 10 s (Box2D v3 726, Rapier 2D 735) and its row 30 spreads 48 mm (70, 64): a pair keeps last step's reference face while the two faces' separations lie within one slop (5 mm), and a clipped point keeps the id of the end it replaces, so resting points keep their warm start. Value clips, relocates, splines, `.abc` layers, implicit shapes, `PointInstancer`, curves and points are not read. A projective `xformOp:transform` is refused. | Those prims are left out or listed in `asset.issues`. | Bake value clips and implicit shapes with `usdcat --flatten` or Blender before loading. |
| UsdSkel (`@margoengine/usdz/skel`, 2026-11-07) | By method: skeletons under a SkelRoot, skin weights, `skel:joints`, `geomBindTransform`, constant and vertex influences, blend shapes with sparse offsets, normal offsets and in-betweens, and their animation as one clip named after the default prim. Measured against OpenUSD 26.08 on 12 real stages: 2.7e-4 of the figure's size at worst, 1.3e-3 on HumanFemale. | The engine takes eight influences on a point. Past that the strongest eight stay and are scaled to the same total, and `asset.issues` says so: that alone is the HumanFemale gap, 0.17 units on a figure 133 units tall (1.5e-5 of its size with the cap lifted). A joint with shear has no node form and is listed. One clip per stage. | Listed in `asset.issues`; the mesh still draws. | Bake to eight influences in the DCC tool. |
| USD time samples (`@margoengine/usdz/anim`, 2026-11-07) | By method: `timeSamples` on `xformOp`s and `visibility`, as one clip per stage; at most 4,096 keys added between two samples. | USD subdivision (`@margoengine/usdz/subdiv`, 2026-11-07) | Enforced: `level` 0 to 6, default 2; a stage over `maxTriangles` gets a lower level for every mesh, and says so. A face that crosses itself stays a fan, as it has no inside to clip. Measured against Blender 5.3: 862 of 862 real meshes within 4.58e-5 of their span at level 2; 346 of 348 stand-in runs of face-varying values at levels 1 and 2. | Refinement runs on the CPU at load. | `triangleSubdivisionRule = "smooth"` refines by the standard rule, with an issue. A value shared by faces that touch only at a point counts as one value: in mode `none` it stays sharp, and Blender gives one such value sharp and the other split, so those two runs differ (10 corners at level 1, up to 2.5e-2). | USD lights and cameras (`@margoengine/usdz/lux`, 2026-11-07) | By method: every area light becomes a punctual one, with no size in the shading; a light's or camera's values are read at the stage's first time, though its transform plays with `/anim`. | MaterialX and Lottie (`@margoengine/loaders/materialx`, `/lottie`, 2026-11-06) | By method: MaterialX converts four surface shaders and the nodes node materials can hold; emission, opacity, procedural nodes, `uvtiling`, includes and custom nodedefs do not convert; shader defaults match the published nodedefs, with `standard_surface` 1.0.0 taken by `version` or `nodedef`, and `realitykit_pbr_surfaceshader` shares the `UsdPreviewSurface` defaults with no published definition checked. | Range cache (`@margoengine/cache/ranges`, 2026-11-07) | Proved in a real browser (Chromium and Edge, 2026-11-07): gltf-pro's own streaming code (`GLTFStream`) reads the real SheenChair.glb through `RangeCache.fetch` with the browser's IndexedDB, and its buffers equal the file cold, offline after a reload and when revalidated; the Node tests cover the rest on stand-ins. Not yet run in a service worker, and not timed. By method: blocks are 64 KiB by default; eviction is per file and reads every file's record (one per file, not per block) before each write; two requests in flight at once that share a block both fetch it. | Blocks let a streamed file be stored as it is read, without the whole file. | A cold request is widened to whole blocks, at most one block more on each side. A request needing a block never fetched fails offline. | Use `AssetCache` to store whole files; a smaller `block` widens requests less. |
| Vary keys (`varyKeys` in `@margoengine/cache/vary`, 2026-11-07) | Proved on stand-ins: an in-memory IndexedDB and a stand-in server in Node; not yet run in a browser. By method: each URL and credential set remembers only the last `Vary` it saw; whether a request sends cookies is judged from its `credentials` mode and origin, as the cookies themselves cannot be read. | A page or worker cannot see cookies, and keeping one `Vary` per URL needs one record, not a list. | Without a `partition`, two users signed in with cookies on one browser profile share entries; after a server changes `Vary`, old entries wait for eviction. | Set `partition` to the signed-in user's id; `delete(url)` drops every entry of a URL. |
| Eviction index (`evictionIndex` in `@margoengine/cache/eviction`, 2026-11-07) | Proved on a real browser's IndexedDB (Chromium and Edge, 2026-11-07), counting the records each write reads: 2,000 files, then 30 writes read 120 records with the index and 60,030 without; not timed. By method: the database moves to IndexedDB version 2, and an AssetCache without the index can no longer open it. | An index on last use is how IndexedDB walks records in order without reading them all; the totals live in two records updated in the same transaction. | Opening such a database without the index sends every request to the network. | Open it with `evictionIndex()` every time, or use a new `name`. |
| Asset bundles (`AssetBundles` in `@margoengine/cache/bundles`, 2026-11-07) | Proved on stand-ins: an AssetCache over an in-memory IndexedDB and a stand-in server in Node; not yet run in a browser. By method: every file of a bundle is hashed once per session when loaded, so a load reads each file's bytes once more on the CPU; a file is stored under its URL plus `?v=<hash>`, so the server must serve that query. | Hashes make a file shared by bundles one stored copy and let a release change only what changed. | A first load each session spends CPU time hashing (SHA-256 in the browser's own crypto). | Leave a file out of the manifest to skip its check; it then caches by URL as plain AssetCache files do. |
| Freshness from Expires and Age (`freshness` of `AssetCache` in `@margoengine/cache`, 2026-11-07) | Proved on stand-ins: an in-memory IndexedDB and a stand-in server in Node; not yet run in a browser. By method: no heuristic freshness from `Last-Modified` (RFC 9111 section 4.2.2), so a file with no `max-age` or `Expires` is revalidated each session; `s-maxage` is ignored, as for any private cache. | A heuristic lifetime would serve files the server never said were fresh. `Age` and `Date` are not CORS-safelisted, so cross-origin they count only when exposed. | Cross-origin without exposed `Age` and `Date`, a file is taken as new when it arrives. | Expose `Age` and `Date` (`Access-Control-Expose-Headers`), or send `max-age`; `freshness: 'max-age'` keeps the old rule. |
| Prioritized prefetch (`Prefetcher`, `throttle` in `@margoengine/cache/prefetch`, 2026-11-07) | Proved on stand-ins: stand-in servers, a stand-in `requestIdleCallback` and an in-memory IndexedDB in Node; not yet run in a browser. By method: `throttle` paces reading of response bodies, not the socket, so it holds the rate only once the browser's receive buffers are full; a priority is fixed once a request starts. | A page cannot set the socket's rate; reading slower makes TCP flow control slow the sender. | The first buffers of a download arrive faster than the cap. | Lower `concurrency`, or `pause()` while the app streams something itself. |

### React page

What a minimal React page downloads, and why it is larger than core + stage (23,797 B gzip). The cube page of the
bundler matrix (`Canvas`, `Mesh`, `BoxGeometry`, `PbrMaterial`, `useFrame`, and `OrbitControls` from
`@margoengine/react/controls`), built by Vite 8.3.4, React 19.3 and `@margoengine/react` installed alone with
`@margoengine/controls` (2026-10-27), measured from the build's source maps (minified bytes per package; gzip is each
package's own gzip size, scaled so the parts add up to the chunk's). Core lights every scene by default
(a sun and an ambient term), so this is also the minimal lit page.

| Part | Minified B | Gzip B | Needed for a lit scene? |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| `react-dom` (client) | 206,925 | 62,263 | Yes: the app's own UI runtime, not Margo's |
| `react` + `scheduler` | 11,635 | 4,430 | Yes: the app's own |
| `@margoengine/core` (engine, renderer, Wasm kernel, camera, shaders, geometry) | 49,485 | 19,056 | Yes |
| `@margoengine/react` (components, internal, assets, the shadows hook) | 14,241 | 5,488 | Yes: `Canvas`, `Mesh` and the hooks |
| `@margoengine/stage` | 2,771 | 1,405 | Not to draw (core draws and lights the cube); `Canvas` wraps its engine in the stage it hands to `onCreated` and `<Stage>` |
| Vite runtime (preload helper, module preload polyfill), app code and `@margoengine/math` (170 B) | 3,135 | 1,609 | The build's own |
| **Entry, requested before the page runs** | **288,234** | **94,251** | Budget 100,000 B gzip |
| `@margoengine/controls/orbit` + its view helpers + profiles, when `OrbitControls` mounts | 17,999 | 6,951 | Yes, for orbiting |
| **Everything the page fetches** | **306,233** | **101,202** | |

React and React DOM are 66% of the page; Margo's part (core, stage, bindings) is 25,949 B gzip (27,028 B before the
stage feature entries and the React subpaths of 2026-10-27, which took 3,089 B of minified loaders out of the stage). Nothing optional is in
the entry: `PbrMaterial` is core's material and pulls in no other package.

- **Fixed (2026-10-26):** `OrbitControls`, `MapControls` and `CadControls` loaded the `@margoengine/controls` index,
  so mounting them fetched TransformControls, DragControls, the gizmo and the `@margoengine/bvh` raycaster as one
  112,655 B (39,072 B gzip) chunk. They now load `@margoengine/controls/orbit` and `/profiles`, `ArcballControls`
  loads `/arcball` and `TransformControls` loads `/transform`: the mount costs 6,951 B gzip, and a Vite build emits
  107,027 B gzip in all instead of 135,875 B.
- **Emitted, never fetched:** the arcball chunk (3,192 B gzip). Nothing else: since 2026-10-27 neither `Canvas` nor
  the stage reaches an optional package, so there are no stand-in stubs either.
- **A textured model** (`<Gltf src="BoxTextured.glb">` from `@margoengine/react/gltf-pro`, with `@margoengine/gltf-pro`
  installed): the entry grows by
  1,750 B gzip (the `Model` binding), and mounting it fetches gltf-pro (175,257 B, 56,074 B gzip: glTF parsing, the
  PBR material and shader, compression hooks) plus the model. The Draco and Basis Wasm are emitted for files that use
  them; this one does not, and the page does not request them.
- **Through `margoengine/react`:** a page emits no Draco or Basis file. `Model`, `Fbx`, `Animation` and the `materials`
  components reach those decoders, so they are separate entries (`margoengine/react/gltf-pro`, `/fbx`, `/animation`,
  `/materials`); Vite copies a `new URL` file when it reads a module, before tree-shaking.
- **Through a kit or `materials`, `animation`, `fbx`:** no Draco or Basis file either. Only the root of `@margoengine/gltf-pro`
  names the decoders; packages that draw models use `@margoengine/gltf-pro/model`, and `loadGLTF` is imported from
  `margoengine/gltf-pro`, not from `margoengine/game`, `/web` or `/viz`.
- Still on the controls index: `PointerLock` (from `@margoengine/react/controls`), because `@margoengine/controls` has no
  pointer-lock entry; a page that does not use it never emits it.

## External video materials (2026-11-08)

`@margoengine/video/material` adds a caller-owned `HTMLVideoElement` or `VideoFrame` to a `Material.features` list. No JS-side frame upload occurs. The browser/driver may still copy or convert internally; platform zero-copy and throughput are unmeasured. A frame is imported per draw, one sampler per device; there are no mipmaps or repeat wrapping. UV0 (default) and UV1 are supported; `flipY` defaults to true, matching Texture's image orientation (first row at v=1); false puts it at v=0. Sources must be ready/open and origin-clean. WebGL2 returns `MargoError` code `unsupported` with a help link. Core's compact material has no feature slot. Custom WGSL must retain the standard surface/base-colour hook. The existing material's own maps, lighting and other features keep their own costs. External textures consume four sampled-texture slots, one implicit sampler and one uniform slot, in addition to the explicit filtering sampler; a fully mapped material can exceed a device's default limits. Alpha affects colour rendering; auxiliary caster/picking passes retain the material's existing alpha inputs. Generated colour frames and a canvas MediaStream on the RTX A6000/Edge prove imports across tasks, no material-path frame uploads and sRGB byte accuracy within 2 of 255 at 1x and 4x MSAA. Real movie files, other adapters, browser-internal copies, speed and custom shader combinations are unmeasured. Run `node scripts/gpu-lock.mjs run --owner=video-check -- node packages/video/test/material-check.mjs` after a package build.

## Page canvas recording (2026-11-08)

`@margoengine/video/record` records origin-clean page canvases with MediaRecorder, on WebGPU, WebGL2 or 2D. Container support and codecs are the browser's choice: default WebM, optional MP4, otherwise coded unsupported with a help link. The caller supplies optional live audio tracks, cloned so originals remain owned by the caller. No audio mixing is performed. All compressed chunks stay in memory until stop. Real-time capture can drop frames or shorten media on a busy/background page; no exact duration/frame count or A/V synchronization bound is claimed. Stop waits for the final chunk; abort, disposal and errors release owned tracks and discard the result. No Node/OffscreenCanvas API or alternate codec fallback is included. The real RTX A6000/Edge check decodes WebM (VP8/Opus) and MP4 (H.264/Opus) from both backends: generated colour and a tone are stand-ins. Other browsers, players, codecs, microphone permission paths and long recordings are unmeasured. Entry 1,140 B gzip; budget 1,396 B. No speed claim. See LIM-571.

## 360 and stereo video (2026-11-08)

`@margoengine/video/360` uses UV0 of `sphereGeometry`, an unlit back-sided material and a camera at its centre. Image centre -Z, right +X, top +Y. Mono (default) spans the whole source; stereo-left-right holds one complete panorama per half, selected explicitly for a screen material (eye left by default). Stereo sources need at least two pixels across, enforced before binding. Sampling clamps half a texel inside each eye; no mips or repeat wrapping. WebGL2 receives coded unsupported with a help link. One video feature per material; playback and source lifetime remain caller-owned. XR reuses native `XRLayers.video` with an equirectangular sphere, automatic compositor eye choice and radius 0 at infinity; it requires the draft WebXR Layers API and XRMediaBinding. Missing XR support propagates the existing XR error. Generated colour panoramas prove six screen directions and both eyes on RTX A6000/Edge; an integrated stand-in session/binding proves XR delegation and layer lifecycle. No headset, real movie, other browser/GPU or speed evidence. Entry 1,694 B gzip, budget 1,881 B. LIM-573.

## Own 2D certified geometry and solver evidence (2026-11-08)

The optional Rust kernel's exact rectangle SAT path requires a current canonical axis rectangle in pair-local
coordinates, finite vertex squared norms at most 2^120 and B-normal squared norms at most 4. The preferred-face
distance certificate additionally requires a coordinate-magnitude bound M in [1,2^20], positive finite A-face
separation and its finite radius/speculation/result checks. These restrict eligibility for an optimization;
all other inputs retain the full prior collision path. [Proof](architecture/physics2d-manifold-proof.md) and
[entry 101](whitepaper/perf-history.md) record the precise guards and unchanged native/Wasm hashes.

The two-point block solver remains production behavior. Earlier per-point alternatives did not meet all contracts
and establish a browser gain. All original accuracy bars remain unchanged. The subsequent sustained-support fix
establishes the required centered 1:1000 contact stack and deliberately re-pins the mixed scene; see the
[support contract](#own-2d-sustained-contact-support). Owned-2D CCD remains separate T-11 / 127.y work, distinct
from existing 1000:1 joint-chain and 3D CCD evidence.
After browser diagnostics: Edge 3.66/1.69/14.52 ms and Firefox 3.50/1.52/11.20 ms for Margo/Box2D/Rapier; separate
loaded sessions cannot prove before/after speed. The Box2D goal remains open and quiet reruns are required.

### Own 2D input validation

The raw Rust kernel under `packages/physics2d/kernel` exposes checked `Result<_, PhysicsError>` body/shape/chain
creation, world stepping and handle operations, bounds queries, scalar/coherent/four-pair and smooth-chain collision.
The public Rust `solver::solve` entry also checks current inputs and derived outputs; its direct-call substep
must be positive and representable. `World::step` retains its validated nonpositive-step no-op policy.
Use `?` to propagate a refusal, or read `PhysicsError::code()` and `help()`; the latter points to this section.
The Rapier-backed TypeScript facade is a separate API. Pure math and mass-property utilities are not all checked
entry points; in particular, `mass::mass_of` retains its direct `MassData` return.

| Code | Refusal |
| --- | --- |
| `PHYSICS2D_NOT_FINITE` | A required finite input or current-state value is NaN or infinite |
| `PHYSICS2D_INVALID_CORE` | An invalid active core count or radius would make collision data unsafe to index or use |
| `PHYSICS2D_DEGENERATE` | A requested shape/chain has insufficient usable geometry |
| `PHYSICS2D_ARITHMETIC_OVERFLOW` | Derived arithmetic cannot represent a required finite value, including positive mass/inertia lost to underflow or an overflowing reciprocal |
| `PHYSICS2D_INVALID_HANDLE` | A body, shape, contact or joint relationship refers outside the current valid objects |
| `PHYSICS2D_INVALID_PARAMETER` | A checked parameter violates its domain, such as negative density, friction or restitution |

Body definitions, collision poses and speculative cutoffs require finite used values. Shape material values are
finite and nonnegative. There is no geometry-independent minimum positive density: shape and aggregate mass,
inertia, moments, centres, extents and required reciprocals must remain representable in their actual arithmetic.
This includes the reciprocal of a positive inverse mass/inertia: a finite first reciprocal can round to a value
whose inverse overflows. Both the rounded centre and reconstructed origin are checked before publication.
Derived contact normal/tangent metrics and their required inverses must also be finite: two individually valid
inverse masses can overflow when added. Such a contact returns `PHYSICS2D_ARITHMETIC_OVERFLOW` before solving.
Computed contact-point relative velocity, normal approach and anchor base are also checked; finite body velocity
alone does not imply a representable `v + w cross r` at a very large contact arm.
Nonzero finite rotation pairs use scale-safe normalization when their squared length overflows or underflows;
ordinary normalization bits are retained. Exact zero pairs in a body definition retain the documented identity
conversion. A directly mutated zero stored body rotation is `PHYSICS2D_INVALID_PARAMETER`; a nonfinite or zero
rotation derived during integration returns the arithmetic error rather than becoming identity or zero silently.
An infinite density and a unit box at `f32::from_bits(1)` are refused before publishing a shape or NaN centre.
Genuine zero density or zero-area geometry keeps its zero-mass behavior; a positive mass/inertia rounded to zero
cannot take that fallback. A dynamic body with no mass retains the existing 1 kg, no-turn fallback.

Body/shape creation and an entire `create_chain` call are transactional for validation/arithmetic failures:
no partial body, shape list, mass state or chain proxies are published, and refused IDs remain available.
`World::step` preflights current public mutable data and relationships before simulation work: body state and
shape lists, current core counts/used vertices/normals/radii, materials/chain ghosts, contact handles/counts/used
values and joint handles/state. A stale broad-phase shape ID is checked before callback indexing. A linear
visitation check over shape references refuses duplicate, missing and foreign-body references.
Used cached normal impulses must be nonnegative. Friction retains the ordinary product/sqrt result when that
product is finite and uses a scale-safe geometric mean when it overflows. Invalid derived scalar or SIMD clamp
bounds propagate to the step's coded arithmetic-error check, rather than asserting inside Rust's clamp.
These checks use current data. Explicit documented sentinels, such as a joint motor's
positive-infinite maximum force for an unlimited motor, remain supported. A later simulation arithmetic error
is returned to the caller; the whole step is not a rollback transaction.

At `47f81f909`, the reproduced collision panic requires both a NaN pose and NaN cutoff: a missing closest-distance
candidate leaves a zero hit mask, whose trailing-zero index escapes the candidate rows. The literal NaN-pose
review call with a finite cutoff returned an empty manifold here. The fix rejects nonfinite public inputs and
checks missing face/distance candidates internally, including the four-pair path; it does not treat invalid
input as an ordinary empty contact. Native regressions cover both forms, overflow, current-array mutations,
creation rollback and valid retained-reference results. Each existing Wasm `check(i)` also exercises invalid
input refusal before comparing the same three production hashes. No hash was re-pinned and no speed result is
claimed. [Reproduce](whitepaper/reproduce.md#own-2d-input-validation) lists the commands and baseline failures.

Input validation closes the input/publication and absent-candidate error class. The separately derived support
correction below establishes the required centered contact bar. Owned-2D CCD is separate T-11 / 127.y work.
