=== Using Margo with AI tools (docs/ai-tools.md) ===

# Using Margo with AI tools

AI coding tools write good Margo code when they read the right pages and check what they wrote. Margo gives them
three ways in, from least to most setup.

## 1. Point the tool at llms.txt

[`llms.txt`](https://margoengine.com/llms.txt) follows the [llms.txt convention](https://llmstxt.org): a title, a
summary, and sections of links with one-line descriptions (guides, one README and one API page per package,
examples). [`llms-full.txt`](https://margoengine.com/llms-full.txt) is the same material as one text file: the
guides in full and each package README (long ones cut, with a link to the rest).

- **Cursor:** Settings, Indexing and Docs, Add Doc, paste `https://margoengine.com/llms-full.txt`. Then write
  `@Docs Margo` in a chat.
- **Claude Code and Claude Desktop:** ask the tool to read `https://margoengine.com/llms.txt` first, or paste the link
  into the chat. Add a line to your project's `CLAUDE.md`: `Margo Engine docs for AI: https://margoengine.com/llms.txt`.
- **Copilot and other chat tools:** attach `llms-full.txt` as a file, or paste the link.

Both files are generated by `node scripts/build-llms.mjs` from the package READMEs, the `api/` reports and `docs/`.
The test `tests/llms.test.js` fails when either is stale. Run the generator after relevant documentation or API
changes; it only updates the files and never commits them.

## 2. Run the MCP server

[`@margoengine/mcp`](../packages/mcp/README.md) is a Model Context Protocol server that runs locally over stdio. It
answers from the docs of the version you installed, and it type-checks code against your project's real Margo types.

| Tool | Use it to |
| --- | --- |
| `search_docs` | Find the API or README section for a task or an exact name. |
| `list_packages` | See which optional package provides a feature (core is frozen; features are packages). |
| `get_package` | Read one package's README or API report. |
| `list_examples` | Find a runnable example before writing one. |
| `check_snippet` | Type-check a snippet strictly against the installed packages. |
| `port_to_margo` | Map a three.js class or task (`OrbitControls`, `InstancedMesh`, "shadow map") to the Margo package and calls, with status, limits and both libraries' code, from the [parity matrix](threejs-parity.md) and [Coming from three.js](from-threejs.md). |
| `explain_error` | Explain a pasted Margo error (the message, its `errors#<id>` link, the id or the `MargoError` code) with its cause and fix from the [error help page](https://margoengine.com/errors). |
| `render_snippet` | Only with `--render`: run a snippet on the GPU in Node and see the PNG it draws. Needs `@margoengine/headless`, `@margoengine/stage` and `webgpu` in the project; runs code with your rights. |

The server also offers every package README and API report and every docs page as resources
(`margo://packages/<id>/readme`, `margo://packages/<id>/api`, `margo://docs/<path>`, `margo://readme`), which a
client can attach to a conversation without a tool call, and four starter prompts: `start_scene`, `port_code`,
`fix_error` and `add_feature` (in Claude Code, `/mcp__margoengine__start_scene` and so on). Each prompt names the
tools to use, in the order below.

Setup (full steps in the [package README](../packages/mcp/README.md)):

```sh
npm i -D @margoengine/mcp typescript margoengine
claude mcp add margoengine -- npx -y @margoengine/mcp        # Claude Code
```

Claude Desktop and Cursor take the same command in a JSON config file: `command` `npx`, `args`
`["-y", "@margoengine/mcp"]` (Claude Desktop also needs `"--root", "/path/to/project"`).

A good loop for an assistant, and the one the server's own instructions suggest: `search_docs` or `list_packages`,
then `get_package` for the package it will use, write the code, then `check_snippet` and fix what it reports before
showing the answer. When the user brings three.js code, `port_to_margo` first, once per class it uses; when they paste a Margo error, `explain_error`.

## 3. Give the assistant a project rule

Short rules in `CLAUDE.md`, `.cursor/rules` or `.github/copilot-instructions.md` stop the most common mistakes:

```md
This project uses Margo Engine (WebGPU). Docs for AI: https://margoengine.com/llms.txt
- Core (`@margoengine/core`) and the stage (`margoengine`) are small; every feature is a separate optional package.
  Find it with the margoengine MCP tool `list_packages` and import only what you use.
- `margoengine/<name>` and `@margoengine/<name>` are the same module.
- Units are metres and glTF conventions (Y up, right-handed).
- Anything that loads or waits takes an `AbortSignal`; errors carry a `code` (branch on it, not the message).
- Run the margoengine `check_snippet` tool on Margo code before presenting it.
```

## What the tools cannot do

- **Render without a GPU binding or a browser page.** `render_snippet` draws in Node through the `webgpu` binding,
  so it needs that package and a GPU (or a software adapter through `gpuFlags`). Code that needs a page (DOM input,
  `createStage('#canvas')`, a frame loop) does not run there: write the snippet against the stage it is given.
- **Run your code by default.** `check_snippet` only compiles; `render_snippet`, which runs code, is offered only when
  the server is started with `--render`.
- **Port by meaning.** `port_to_margo` matches the words and name parts of the matrix rows. A class the matrix does not
  list gets no row; the answer says so and points at `search_docs`.
- **Watch the docs change.** Resources come from the snapshot the package was built with, so there are no
  subscriptions or change notifications; update `@margoengine/mcp` to get newer docs.
- **Know a package you have not installed.** `check_snippet` resolves imports from your `node_modules`; an import of a
  package that is not installed is reported as an error, which is the right answer for an app that does not have it.

## Keeping it current

| File | Made by | Checked by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `site/llms.txt`, `site/llms-full.txt` | `node scripts/build-llms.mjs` | `tests/llms.test.js` (in `npm run verify`) and `node scripts/build-llms.mjs --check` |
| `margoengine.com/llms/...` pages | `scripts/build-site.js` | `npm run site:check` |
| `@margoengine/mcp` corpus | `packages/mcp/scripts/build-corpus.mjs`, at package build | `packages/mcp/tests/` |

=== margoengine (packages/margoengine/README.md) ===

# margoengine

Margo Engine in one install. The root is the stage (`createStage`, everything `@margoengine/core` exports), and every
engine package is a subpath: `margoengine/gltf`, `margoengine/shadows`, `margoengine/physics`, `margoengine/react`,
including their smaller entries (`margoengine/controls/orbit`, `margoengine/geometry/primitives`, ...).

The packages are not on npm yet: `npm i margoengine` gets only a name placeholder (0.0.1, no engine) until 1.0.0 is published. Use the clone or local-tarball routes in the [Install](../../README.md#install) section until then.

```ts
import {createStage} from 'margoengine';
import {Shadows} from 'margoengine/shadows';
import {OrbitControls} from 'margoengine/controls/orbit';

const stage = await createStage('#viewport', {controls: false});
const shadows = Shadows.attach(stage.engine, {resolution: 2048});
const ground = stage.box({size: [10, 0.2, 10], color: '#c8c8c8'});
const cube = stage.box({position: [0, 1, 0], color: '#84d6bd'});
shadows.add(ground);
shadows.add(cube);
const controls = new OrbitControls(stage.engine.camera, stage.engine.canvas as HTMLCanvasElement);
stage.onTick((delta) => {
  cube.rotation.y += delta;
  controls.update(delta);
});
```

## You load only what you import

`margoengine/<name>` is a one-line re-export of `@margoengine/<name>`, the same module with the same classes, and
every file is free of side effects. An app that imports `margoengine/shadows` bundles exactly the bytes it would bundle
from `@margoengine/shadows` (`tests/umbrella.test.js` compares the two bundles); the other packages are installed but
never loaded. `import {createStage} from 'margoengine'` is core + stage alone, 23,797 B gzip.

Use either name; they are interchangeable. Each package is still published on its own (`@margoengine/shadows`) for
apps that want a smaller install.

## Short names

```ts
import * as M from 'margoengine';
import * as Physics from 'margoengine/physics';

const stage = await M.createStage('#viewport');
const mesh = stage.box({color: '#84d6bd'});
mesh.position.y = 1;
const cubes: M.Mesh[] = [mesh];          // types come along: M.Mesh, M.Vec3, Physics.PhysicsOptions
console.log(cubes.length, typeof Physics.Physics);
```

A namespace import tree-shakes like named imports in every modern bundler: only the members you use are kept.

## Third-party libraries

Two packages use a library you install yourself, only when you use that package. Everything else is in the one
install.

| Package | Install | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `margoengine/physics` | `npm i @dimforge/rapier3d-compat` | The solver; `await Physics.load()` readies it once per app |
| `margoengine/react` | `npm i react react-dom` | It is a React component library |

`margoengine/react` holds every React binding but five groups, each its own entry: `margoengine/react/gltf-pro`
(`Model`, `Gltf`), `/fbx`, `/animation`, `/materials` and `/physics`. The first four reach the Draco and Basis decoders,
and Vite copies a decoder's Wasm into the build as soon as it reads the module, used or not. A page that imports none
of them builds with no Wasm of theirs:

```tsx
import { Canvas, Mesh, BoxGeometry } from 'margoengine/react';
import { Model } from 'margoengine/react/gltf-pro'; // only on a page that loads a model
```

The kits `margoengine/game`, `/web` and `/viz` include `loadGLTF`, so their builds hold the decoder files; the browser
fetches them only for a file that uses Draco or KTX2.

Without them nothing else changes; the package that needs one says which to install when you use it.

=== @margoengine/stage (packages/stage/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/stage

You normally use this package as [`margoengine`](../margoengine/README.md): `import {createStage} from 'margoengine'` is this package. The packages are not on npm yet; see the [Install](../../README.md#install) section for the routes that work today.

High-level setup for Margo Engine. Mount a canvas, enable orbit/pan/zoom, start rendering and create a spinning orb in five lines. The stage creates a WebGPU engine. Pass `fallback` from the optional `@margoengine/webgl2-compat/preview` when a browser has no WebGPU; without it, creation rejects with `WebGPU unavailable`. Core handles resize and automatically recovers a lost WebGPU device. A lost WebGL2 context reports through `onError` and stops rendering; dispose and recreate the stage to resume.

This package is built from source alongside the engine. See the [package catalog](../../docs/README.md) for npm availability. Run `npm run build:packages` in the repository, or install its local tarball and `@margoengine/core`. The only dependency is `@margoengine/core`. `@margoengine/gltf`, `@margoengine/creative`, `@margoengine/scenery`, `@margoengine/gltf-pro`, `@margoengine/environment`, `@margoengine/staging`, `@margoengine/shadows`, `@margoengine/tonemap`, `@margoengine/xr`, `@margoengine/physics`, `@dimforge/rapier3d-compat` and `@margoengine/save` are optional peers, used only by the feature entries below. The root entry imports none of them, not even lazily, so any bundler (Vite, Rollup, esbuild, webpack, Turbopack) builds an app that installs only this package and core. Each feature entry imports its package on the first call and rejects with `Install <package>` when it is absent, which keeps that code out of the initial scene.

Apps using Stage load this facade and its shared core, then only the feature entries they use and those features' required dependencies. Apps using the Engine API directly can load core without Stage. Choose specific feature imports and load heavier features on demand; keep one matching core version across the app.

The build requires the combined core and stage facade, with every base export retained, to stay strictly below 25,000 bytes gzip. It writes measurements to `test-results/modern-bundle-sizes.json`; `npm run measure:size` repeats the gate against the built artifacts. Lazy features and application bootstrap/chunk overhead are measured separately; this is not the complete page download size.

Give the container a height, for example `<div id="scene" style="height:400px"></div>`:

```ts
import {createStage} from 'margoengine';
const app = await createStage('#scene');
const orb = app.sphere({color: '#84d6bd', roughness: 0.25, scale: [1, 0.85, 1]});
app.onTick(delta => {orb.rotation.z += delta;});
window.addEventListener('pagehide', () => app.dispose(), {once: true});
```

Use a selector, an HTMLElement container or an existing canvas. The wrapper appends its own accessible canvas to containers. `app.dispose()` stops rendering, aborts active imports, removes controls and removes an owned canvas. Existing canvases and their styles remain available after disposal. Call disposal when your page or component unmounts. `onTick` returns an unsubscribe function.

`createStage(target, options)` accepts core camera/backend/capacity options and `controls`, `autoStart`, `label` and `onError`. Controls and rendering start by default. Use `autoStart: false` for manual rendering through `app.engine`. Camera validation and initial rendering finish before creation resolves.

| API | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `app.sphere({radius, segments, ...options})` | Creates an orb with the same material/transform options as boxes |
| `app.box({size, color, roughness, metalness, position, rotation, scale, parent, name})` | Creates a box and returns the existing mutable mesh handle |
| `app.mesh(geometry, options)` | Attaches existing or custom geometry with the same options |
| `app.onTick(delta => { ... })` | Runs once per frame with delta in seconds; returns an unsubscribe function |
| `app.fit()` / `app.fit(model.meshes)` | Fits visible geometry, including world transforms and hierarchy |
| `app.use(plugin)` | Attaches an existing plugin and returns it |
| `app.signal` | An `AbortSignal` that aborts when the stage is disposed; the feature entries combine it with yours |
| `app.engine` | Existing core API: camera, picking, plugins, manual render, start/stop and recovery |

## CAD camera controls

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/stage.md]

=== @margoengine/core (packages/core/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/core

Import `margoengine/core` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/core` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

WebGPU rendering (WebGL2 fallback via the optional `@margoengine/webgl2-compat/preview`), a deterministic Rust/Wasm transform kernel, instanced drawing of one directional GGX light on position and normal, reversed float depth and picking. Materials are color, roughness, and metalness.

Desktop scenes use 4× MSAA with a canvas DPR cap of 1; phones use single-sample rendering with a DPR cap of 2. For slower desktop GPUs, set `globalThis.margoLow` to a pixel ratio (for example `1` or `1.5`) before creating the engine: scenes then render single-sampled with the DPR capped at that value, which on an Intel Arc 140V laptop cut the island demo's GPU frame from about 20 to 10 ms (particles off) compared with 4× MSAA. The site demos choose this light tier by measuring the GPU rather than guessing from the device. Color and depth targets follow canvas resize. Optional scene captures retain that sampling policy and expose single-sample resolved textures. CSS layout and HTML text retain native density.

`engine.pick(x, y)` updates scene state without forcing a color frame. One readback runs at a time and overlapping calls wait their turn, so a loop of picks costs one readback a point; `pickMany` of `@margoengine/selection` answers many points from one. For cached forward-pass IDs, instance culling in a 3×3 micro frustum and neighbor resolution, attach the optional `Picking` plugin from `@margoengine/selection`. On a canvas without client size (an `OffscreenCanvas` in a worker) pick coordinates are canvas pixels.

Static scenes cost little per frame: the kernel recomputes only entities whose position, rotation, scale, parent, bounds or visibility changed (and their descendants); the engine reuses last frame's instance list unless the mesh set, a geometry or material assignment, a material's values or the layers changed; a mesh that culling or `visible` shows or hides moves one row of its batch (shown: the batch's next row; hidden: the batch's last row takes its place), a moved mesh rewrites its own row, and the WebGPU renderer uploads only the changed rows, one `writeBuffer` for each run of neighbouring rows. On an Intel Arc 140V laptop the kernel part made the kernel 2.6-4x cheaper and let 50,000 CAD parts orbit at 92 FPS instead of 49 (CAD measurements, before the row change). An orbiting camera no longer re-collects every frame: with 50,000 boxes and 500 culling flips a frame, the frame does 50,000 byte compares, 1,000 map lookups, 12,000 float copies and uploads 48 KB in at most 500 writes, where it did 100,000 lookups, 1.2 million float copies and a 4.8 MB upload (counted in `tests/core-instance-cache.test.js`; not timed yet). Several cameras on one scene flip most rows, and then cost what a full collection costs. Draw order among the instances of one geometry follows these row moves, so it changes after a flip; opaque pixels are the same except for two core meshes at exactly the same depth. Contract for `@margoengine/core/extension` users: the per-geometry instance buffers (`engine.geometryBuffers(geometry).instance`) belong to core and are read-only for packages (bind them, never write them, except a package that claims a batch and uploads its changed rows with `uploadRows`, see "Bulk poses and instance rows"; use your own buffer, as `@margoengine/selection`'s micro pick pass does), and `store.matrices` is kernel output (change transforms through the mesh, never by writing world matrices). GPU culling of core meshes (`@margoengine/culling`'s `CulledMeshes`) uses one hook: passes see the frame's batches as `context.batches`, and a package may set `batch.redirect = {instances, args}` for the frame; every core draw of that batch (main pass and replays) then reads the package's compacted instance records and `drawIndexedIndirect` arguments instead of core's buffer and count. Core still uploads into its own instance buffer, which stays the read-only source the package culls from. `engine.start({culling: false})` skips core's CPU frustum test in the built-in loop (as `render({culling: false})` does for one frame) when a package culls on the GPU.

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/core.md]

=== @margoengine/math (packages/math/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/math

Import `margoengine/math` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/math` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

Vector2, Vector3, Vector4, Quaternion, Euler, Matrix3, Matrix4, Color, Box3, OBB, Line3, Triangle, Capsule, Sphere, Plane, Ray, Frustum, Spherical, Cylindrical, SH3, MathUtils and the project functions. Methods write into `this` (chainable) or an `out` argument instead of returning new objects; only `clone()` and `toArray()` with no target return new ones.

```ts
import {Vector3, Quaternion, Euler, Color} from 'margoengine/math';
import {Engine} from 'margoengine/core';
import {createMesh} from 'margoengine/materials';
import {box} from 'margoengine/core';
const engine = await Engine.create(document.querySelector('canvas')!);
const mesh = engine.createMesh().setGeometry(box());
const position = new Vector3(0, 1, 0).addScaledVector(new Vector3(1, 0, 0), 2);
mesh.setPosition(position.toArray()).setQuaternion(new Quaternion().setFromEuler(new Euler(0, Math.PI / 4, 0)).toArray());
engine.camera.position = new Vector3().copy(mesh.position).add(new Vector3(0, 2, 5)).toArray();
new Color('#ff8800').toArray(mesh.material.data); // linear RGB, recolors in place
```

Each type is its own module: `import {Vector3} from '@margoengine/math/vector3'` (or from the root, which tree-shakes the same) ships about 1.3 kB min+gzip. The whole package is about 10.4 kB min+gzip ([entry-sizes.json](../../examples/package-benchmarks/results/entry-sizes.json)).

Array helpers: the other Margo packages work on plain arrays (`number[]`, `Float32Array`, `Float64Array`) rather than these classes, and share one copy of those helpers from here, each bundled into the package that uses it. `@margoengine/math/mat4`: `multiplyMatrices(a, b, out)`, `invertMatrix(m, out)` (cofactors), `invertMatrixStable(m, out, workspace?)` (pivoted, rejects non-finite input and Float32 overflow; `out` may be `m`) and `composeMatrix(t, q, s, out)`, column-major like `camera.matrix`, float64 arithmetic; the inverses return null (`out` untouched) when they fail. `@margoengine/math/quat`: `eulerToQuaternion(x, y, z)` (XYZ, like `Mesh.setRotation`), `multiplyQuaternions(a, b)`, `axisAngleToQuaternion(axis, angle)`, `conjugateQuaternion(q)`, `normalizeQuaternion(q)` and `rotateByQuaternion(v, q)`, returning new arrays, and `rotationToQuaternion(m, out?, sx?, sy?, sz?)`: the rotation of a column-major 3x3 or 4x4 (columns divided by the given scales; a negative `sx` undoes a mirror), the one conversion every package uses.

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/math.md]

=== @margoengine/quality (packages/quality/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/quality

Import `margoengine/quality` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/quality` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

Measured quality tiers. Desktops start on a light tier (single-sampled, pixel ratio capped, paced to an even rate of at
least 60 FPS) and read the real GPU time of each frame by timestamp queries; a page under the limit gets the full 4× MSAA tier
from its next load. No PC is first shown the 4× tier or reloaded by the probe (the light tier's own frame rate depends on
the GPU), and no rule based on device names is involved.

```ts
import {applyQualityTier, paceEngine, watchQuality} from 'margoengine/quality';
import {Engine} from 'margoengine/core';
const canvas = document.querySelector('canvas')!;

applyQualityTier();                       // before creating the engine
const engine = await Engine.create(canvas, {backend: 'webgpu'});
paceEngine(engine);                       // light tier: an even rate of at least 60 FPS
// ...build the scene and start rendering, then:
watchQuality();
```

- `applyQualityTier()` returns `'light'`, `'high'` or `'phone'`. Phones are single-sampled with the pixel ratio capped
  at 1 (`globalThis.margoLow = 1`), even with `?quality=high` or `?scale=2`. It sets core's `globalThis.margoLow`, which
  core reads when it builds pipelines and sizes the canvas, so it must run before the engine is created.
- `watchQuality()` reads 120 frames on the light tier and, when the 90th percentile of the time a frame's GPU passes cover (passes that run side by side count once) is under
  `FAST_GPU_MS` (8 ms), remembers `'high'` for this page in `localStorage['margoQuality:' + location.pathname]`. One key
  per page, because the result says what this page's scene costs: a light scene must not mark a weak PC high for a heavy
  one. A slow reading remembers nothing, so one bad session cannot hold a browser on the light tier: the next load
  measures again. On the full tier, five consecutive seconds under 55 FPS remember that for good (`'held'`) and reload
  once (a machine that slowed down, for example on battery).
- Timestamps: `applyQualityTier()` adds `timestamp-query` to the devices this page asks for, only while the page is still
  to be measured, until `watchQuality()` starts. The reading is its own small chunk, downloaded only by a page that reads. During the reading (about 4 s at 60 FPS, 10 s at most) `submit` and
  `createCommandEncoder` are wrapped and every pass gets timestamp writes; then all of it is put back and its GPU objects
  destroyed, so nothing runs after the reading. Without `timestamp-query` the page stays light and stores nothing. A frame
  whose passes the page times itself is not counted. Copies between passes, presenting and other work between passes are
  not in the number.
- `onReading(milliseconds)` on `watchQuality` reports the reading when it ends, undefined when there is none.
- For testing: `?quality=high` or `?quality=low` forces a tier without remembering it; `?scale=1.5` sets the light
  tier's pixel ratio (1 to 2). `localStorage.removeItem('margoQuality:' + location.pathname)` measures again.
- `paceEngine(engine)` sets core's `engine.pace` hook on the light tier so `engine.start()` renders at an even rate of
  at least 60 FPS instead of swinging between 120 and 40 FPS on a slow GPU. Each frame spans the most whole refreshes that
  still reach 60, so the rate depends on the display:

  | Display | 60 Hz | 75 Hz | 90 Hz | 100 Hz | 120 Hz | 144 Hz | 165 Hz | 200 Hz | 240 Hz |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | Frames per second | 60 | 75 | 90 | 100 | 60 | 72 | 83 | 67 | 60 |

  Other tiers stay uncapped. Nothing global is patched: other `requestAnimationFrame` loops on the page run at the display
  rate. An app that renders from its own loop (calling `engine.render` itself) can gate it with `frameDue`.
- `capFrameRate(engine, rate = 60)` sets the same pacing on any engine regardless of tier. It reads the display's refresh
  from the last 16 callback gaps, so it follows a page moved to another display within 16 frames.
- The light-tier reading skips the first two seconds and gives up after ten, at any refresh rate.

## Dynamic resolution

```ts
import {applyQualityTier, watchResolution} from 'margoengine/quality';
import {Engine} from 'margoengine/core';
const canvas = document.querySelector('canvas')!;
applyQualityTier(); // light or phone tier
const engine = await Engine.create(canvas, {backend: 'webgpu'});
using resolution = watchResolution({budget: 12, min: 0.6}); // restores full resolution when disposed
console.log(resolution.scale);
```

=== @margoengine/webgl2-compat (packages/webgl2-compat/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/webgl2-compat


This is the single WebGL2 package. Use the root `install()` entry to run the real
renderer without WebGPU. The optional `/preview`, `/pick`, `/restore` and `/auto`
entries preserve the smaller preview for lower-tier WebGL2. The former webgl
workspace and its umbrella aliases were removed before release; use the entries
and examples below.

Import `margoengine/webgl2-compat` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/webgl2-compat` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

**Status: milestones M0 to M8 of the [roadmap](../../docs/webgl2-compat-roadmap.md) done.** This layer is the site's fallback: every live demo on margoengine.com loads it when the browser has no WebGPU. Of the 27 site demos, 20 draw the same pixels as native WebGPU and 7 run with one accepted difference (WebGL2 cannot read one sample of a multisampled texture); all 32 Khronos gallery models draw the same pixels ([webgl2-compat-demos.md](../../docs/webgl2-compat-demos.md) lists each one). The voxel path tracer refuses the layer (MargoError `unsupported`); XR runs on it through the [`/xr` entry](#xr-margoenginewebgl2-compatxr). Not done: the frame-budget run on an integrated GPU is not recorded yet, and a transform-feedback tier for own-index compute stores is parked (speed only, those stores already run on the scatter tier with the same pixels). The small preview is now the optional `/preview` entry of this package. This package
is the WebGL2 compatibility layer for browsers without WebGPU: a WebGPU-shaped device built on WebGL2 that translates
every WGSL shader to GLSL ES 3.00, so core and the packages run their usual WebGPU code unchanged. Today core renders
on it (meshes, instancing, 4x MSAA and exact-pixel mode, several views, picking and device loss) with the same pixels
as native WebGPU on the same GPU, and so do the render checks of materials (its compute scenarios included), glTF
PBR, lines, points, text, lod and the skinned shadow check. Render shaders read storage buffers, and compute pipelines
run (milestone M5): as fragment draws, as point draws, or on the CPU, whichever the shader allows (see Compute below).
Packages whose WebGPU route would be slow there take a route of their own (milestone M6, see Package routes below).
Render shaders that write storage buffers or textures are refused with MargoError code `unsupported`: WebGL2 render
shaders cannot write them.

Load it only where WebGPU is missing, with a dynamic import, so browsers with WebGPU never download it:

```ts
import { Engine } from 'margoengine/core';

const canvas = document.querySelector('canvas') as HTMLCanvasElement;
const webgpu = 'gpu' in navigator && (await navigator.gpu.requestAdapter()) !== null;
if (!webgpu) await (await import('margoengine/webgl2-compat')).install();
const engine = await Engine.create(canvas);
engine.render();
```

`install()` makes `navigator.gpu` a WebGPU-shaped GPU on WebGL2, makes `canvas.getContext('webgpu')` return its canvas
context, defines `GPUBufferUsage` and the other flag objects where the browser lacks them, and names its classes as
the WebGPU interfaces (`GPUBuffer`, `GPUDevice` and the rest) while installed, so `instanceof GPUBuffer` holds for its
objects, also in a browser that defines those interfaces without an adapter. Where the browser's own
WebGPU has an adapter it does nothing (it resolves `{ installed: false, reason: 'webgpu' }`) unless you pass
`{ force: true }`, which the layer's tests use to compare both paths on one machine. It rejects with MargoError code
`unsupported` on a browser whose WebGL2 is below the full tier, naming what is missing. `uninstall()` puts everything
back. The root entry holds only the probe below and `install()`: the device, the GLSL back end and the WGSL front end
load inside `install()`.

What it does:

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/webgl2-compat.md]

=== @margoengine/worker (packages/worker/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/worker

Runs the engine inside a Web Worker on an `OffscreenCanvas`, so a heavy scene never blocks the page's main thread and a busy page never stalls the scene. The helper moves the canvas and keeps the worker told of the page's canvas: its size, position, pixel ratio and visibility, and the input events the worker listens for. Core needs no change and no option: `Engine.create`, `engine.pick`, the frame loop, control packages and the `@margoengine/webgl2-compat/preview` fallback run on the received canvas as they do on the page.

Two entries, one per side. `@margoengine/worker` goes in the page and `@margoengine/worker/canvas` in the worker, so neither side downloads the other's code.

```ts
// page.ts
import { transferCanvas, workerCanvasSupported } from '@margoengine/worker';

const canvas = document.querySelector('canvas')!;
if (!workerCanvasSupported()) throw new Error('Run the scene on the page here');
const worker = new Worker(new URL('./scene-worker.js', import.meta.url), { type: 'module' });
const view = await transferCanvas(canvas, worker, { data: { level: 'plaza' } });

// Later: `view.dispose()` disposes the engine in the worker, then the worker is yours to end.
addEventListener('pagehide', () => {
  view.dispose();
  worker.terminate();
});
```

```ts
// scene-worker.ts
import { box, Engine, PbrMaterial } from '@margoengine/core';
import { OrbitControls } from '@margoengine/controls';
import { receiveCanvas } from '@margoengine/worker/canvas';

const received = await receiveCanvas();
const engine = await Engine.create(received.canvas);
received.attach(engine);
engine.createMesh().setGeometry(box()).setMaterial(new PbrMaterial({ color: '#84d6bd' }));
const controls = new OrbitControls(engine.camera, received.canvas);
engine.onFrame((_, delta) => controls.update(delta));
engine.start();
```

## Page side

`transferCanvas(canvas, worker, options)` resolves with a `WorkerCanvas` once the worker holds the canvas. Either side may start first.

| Option | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `data` | `undefined` | Anything structured clone accepts, read in the worker as `received.data`. |
| `transfer` | `[]` | Objects in `data` to transfer instead of copy. |
| `signal` | none | Aborts the wait. A canvas that had not moved yet stays usable. |
| `timeout` | `30000` | Milliseconds to wait for the worker to call `receiveCanvas`. |

It rejects with a `MargoError` whose `code` is `unsupported` (the browser cannot move a canvas), `state` (the canvas has a context or already moved), `failed` (the worker's script failed) or `timeout`.

`view.dispose()`, or `using`, stops forwarding, aborts `received.signal` and disposes an engine that used `received`. A canvas cannot come back from a worker, and the worker keeps running until you call `worker.terminate()`. `workerCanvasSupported()` says whether the browser can do this at all.

Your own `worker.postMessage` traffic is left alone: the link runs on a `MessageChannel` of its own after a short handshake whose messages carry the key `margo-worker-canvas`. Errors in the worker reach `worker.addEventListener('error', ...)`; the engine's default `onError` reports them there.

## Worker side

`receiveCanvas({signal, timeout})` resolves with a `ReceivedCanvas`:

| Member | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `canvas` | The `OffscreenCanvas`, with `clientWidth`, `clientHeight`, `getBoundingClientRect`, `style` and the pointer capture methods of the page's canvas. Typed as an element, so it passes to `Engine.create` and to controls. |
| `data` | The page's `data` option. |
| `hidden` | True while the page is hidden. |
| `signal` | Aborts when the page disposes its end. |

`received.attach(engine)` makes the first frame after a background tab step 0, as on the page, and lets the page dispose the engine.

Because `clientWidth` follows the page and the page's `devicePixelRatio` and `margoLow` are copied to the worker, the engine picks the same drawing-buffer size as on the page, and `engine.pick` takes CSS pixels. With `exactSize` the worker owns `canvas.width` and `canvas.height`.

Input events arrive on `received.canvas`, as plain events with the values of the real ones (`clientX`, `pointerId`, `deltaY`, `key`, ...). The page only forwards a type once something in the worker listens for it. Pointer, mouse, wheel, click, context menu and focus events come from the canvas; key events come from the document, since an unfocused canvas gets none, and they land on `received.canvas`, which is where controls listen when an element has no document. A `style` written in the worker (`touchAction`, `cursor`) is set on the page's canvas.

## What differs from the page

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/worker.md]

=== @margoengine/stats (packages/stats/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/stats

Import `margoengine/stats` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/stats` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

Zero runtime dependencies. Frame sampling uses a fixed Float64Array ring.
`tick(milliseconds, drawCalls?, dispatches?)` performs numeric updates only;
DOM strings and canvas drawing refresh separately every 150 ms. Encoder/pass wrappers
and asynchronous GPU readback allocate outside `tick`.

```ts
import {Stats} from 'margoengine/stats';
import type {EngineKernel} from 'margoengine/core';
function attach(engine: EngineKernel) {
  return Stats.attach(engine, {samples: 120, profiling: true});
}
```

GPU memory and a JSON report are in their own entry:

```ts
import {Engine} from 'margoengine/core';
import {Stats} from 'margoengine/stats';
import {GPUMemory, statsReport} from 'margoengine/stats/report';

const engine = await Engine.create(document.querySelector('canvas')!);
const memory = GPUMemory.attach(engine.gpu!);   // counts what is made from now on
const stats = Stats.attach(engine);
memory.view(stats);                             // a row in the panel
engine.start();
console.log(JSON.stringify(statsReport(stats, memory)));
```

Sizes come from the descriptors, so driver padding is not in them, and objects made before `attach` are not seen.

Pipeline compile tracking is in its own entry. It shows which shader and pipeline compiles ran near a slow frame, and when. Read a hitch as evidence, not proof: times are CPU time around each call, and browsers compile in another process, so that is the most a page can see. It sees only what is compiled after it starts, so use `trackNext` below to include the engine's startup pipelines:

```ts
import {Engine} from 'margoengine/core';
import {Stats} from 'margoengine/stats';
import {PipelineCompiles} from 'margoengine/stats/compile';

const engine = await Engine.create(document.querySelector('canvas')!);
const compiles = PipelineCompiles.attach(engine, {hitchMilliseconds: 33.4});
compiles.view(Stats.attach(engine));            // totals and the newest hitch in the panel
compiles.onHitch((hitch) => {
  console.warn(`${hitch.milliseconds.toFixed(1)} ms frame near`, hitch.compiles.map((record) => record.label));
});
engine.start();
console.log(JSON.stringify(compiles));          // every record and hitch, when you want them
```

Each record has `kind` (`'shader'`, `'render'` or `'compute'`), `label`, `blocking` (false for the `...Async` calls), `startedAt`, `frame`, `milliseconds` (null while an async call runs) and `failed`. A frame over `hitchMilliseconds` (default 33.4) with compiles in it or in the frame before is a hitch, with `frame`, `at`, `milliseconds` and `compiles`, blocking calls first and then the longest. `capacity` (default 256) is how many records and hitches stay; `count` goes on counting. Label your pipelines to read this easily, or pass `stacks: true` (default false) to keep where each call came from.

To see the engine's own startup pipelines as well, start before the engine does:

```ts
import {Engine} from 'margoengine/core';
import {PipelineCompiles} from 'margoengine/stats/compile';

const compiles = new PipelineCompiles().trackNext(); // catches the next device this page makes
const engine = await Engine.create(document.querySelector('canvas')!);
engine.use(compiles);
console.log(compiles.toJSON().count, 'compiles so far');
```

It follows the engine's device through a device restore and sees only what is compiled after `attach`, or after `trackNext`. Times are CPU time around each call. Browsers compile in another process, so a blocking call can return quickly and the stall arrives later, which is why the frame before counts too. A hitch is evidence that a compile was near a slow frame, not proof that it was the cause. With your own loop, call `compiles.track(device)` and `compiles.frame(milliseconds)` once per frame.

The CPU phase breakdown times the kernel tick, culling, encoding and submit of each frame:

```ts
import {Engine} from 'margoengine/core';
import {Stats} from 'margoengine/stats';
import {FramePhases} from 'margoengine/stats/phases';

const engine = await Engine.create(document.querySelector('canvas')!);
const phases = FramePhases.attach(engine, {samples: 120});
phases.view(Stats.attach(engine));              // the averages in the panel
engine.start();
setInterval(() => console.log(phases.last.encode, phases.average().tick), 1000);
```

All numbers are CPU milliseconds, and they add up to `total`:

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/stats.md]

=== @margoengine/inspector (packages/inspector/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/inspector

Import `margoengine/inspector` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/inspector` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

Optional DOM inspector for core entities, including `stage.engine`. The hierarchy
updates as entities are added, renamed, reparented or disposed. Arrow keys select,
expand and collapse tree items. Selected entities expose visibility, local
transforms and their core PBR material's roughness and metallic values. Editing a
shared material changes every mesh using it.

```ts
import {Inspector} from 'margoengine/inspector';
import type {EngineKernel} from 'margoengine/core';
function attach(engine: EngineKernel, effects: {exposure: number; bloom: number}) {
  return Inspector.attach(engine, {effects});
}
```

Pass the mutable options object of your attached post-processing effect to
`effects`; exposure/bloom controls bind directly to it. Unbound controls are disabled.

## Place the panel in your page layout

By default the panel is a `position: fixed` element at the top right of the page with a high `z-index`. In an app with
its own buttons in that corner it sits on top of them and takes their clicks. Give it a container with `parent`, and
override its position with a style on `inspector.element` (a style set there wins over the panel's built-in one):

```ts
import {Inspector} from 'margoengine/inspector';
import type {EngineKernel} from 'margoengine/core';
function attachInSidebar(engine: EngineKernel, sidebar: HTMLElement) {
  const inspector = Inspector.attach(engine, {parent: sidebar});
  Object.assign(inspector.element.style, {
    position: 'relative', top: 'auto', right: 'auto', width: '100%', maxHeight: '70vh', overflow: 'auto',
  });
  return inspector;
}
```

The panel then sits in the flow of `sidebar` with a bounded height and scrolls inside it. The
[debugging guide](../../docs/guides/debugging.md) runs this in a real browser and clicks the button next to the panel.

## Edit, undo, search, pick, save

Every change made in the panel (name, visibility, position, rotation, scale, colour, double sided, roughness, metallic,
bound effects) is recorded and can be undone with the Undo and Redo buttons, `Ctrl/Cmd+Z`, `Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+Z` or
`Ctrl/Cmd+Y` (inside a text field the browser keeps its own undo). A slider drag is one step. The Search box keeps the
entities whose name contains the text, and their parents. A click on the canvas selects the object under the pointer
(`pick: false` turns it off; a pointer that moves more than 4 px is a camera drag, not a click). Colour edits the core
material's base colour (sRGB in the panel, linear in the material).

```ts
import {Inspector} from 'margoengine/inspector';
import type {EngineKernel} from 'margoengine/core';
async function tour(engine: EngineKernel) {
  const inspector = Inspector.attach(engine, {historyLimit: 500});
  const saved = JSON.stringify(inspector.snapshot());   // names, visibility, transforms, material values
  // ...edit in the panel or in code...
  inspector.restore(JSON.parse(saved));                 // one undoable step; checks the file first
  inspector.undo();
  inspector.redo();
  console.log(inspector.resources());                   // meshes, geometries, materials, triangles, plugins
  console.log(inspector.shaderSource.length);           // the scene WGSL of the latest WebGPU frame
  inspector.history.onChange(() => console.log(inspector.history.nextUndo));
}
```

The panel's Save button downloads the snapshot as `scene.json` and Load restores one. `restore` matches meshes by id,
reports the ones that are gone (`missing`), changes nothing when the file is malformed or the engine rejects a value
(a scale of 0), and does not recreate or reparent meshes. The Resources section counts what the engine draws, and Scene
shader shows the WGSL of the latest WebGPU frame; both build their text only while open. Without the panel, import
`EditHistory` from `margoengine/inspector/history`, `snapshotMeshes`/`restoreSnapshot`/`parseSnapshot` from
`margoengine/inspector/snapshot` and `describeEngine` from `margoengine/inspector/resources`.

Not included: creating or deleting entities, reparenting, shader editing and a GPU memory view (WebGPU does not report
resource sizes). Other packages' lights, materials, shadows and effects are edited in the package panel below.

## Edit other packages' objects

=== @margoengine/gltf (packages/gltf/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/gltf

Import `margoengine/gltf` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/gltf` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

Lazy static glTF/GLB loading, named nodes and shared primitive geometry for Margo Engine.

Package name: `@margoengine/gltf`, version `1.0.0`. Build from source or install a local tarball until the renamed package is published.

```sh
npm install @margoengine/core@1.0.0 @margoengine/gltf@1.0.0
```

```ts
import { Engine } from 'margoengine/core';
import { loadGLTF } from 'margoengine/gltf';

const canvas = document.querySelector<HTMLCanvasElement>('canvas')!;
const engine = await Engine.create(canvas);
const model = await loadGLTF(engine, '/model.glb');
engine.start();
// On teardown: model.dispose(); engine.dispose();
```

## Optional features

The root loader reads static models with float positions and constant colours. Each feature below is its own entry, so
a file that needs none of them costs none of their bytes. Pass the ones you want in `extensions`, to `loadGLTF` or
`parseGLTF`; they combine. A file needing something no entry covers still throws, with a pointer to `@margoengine/gltf-pro`.

### Quantized meshes

`@margoengine/gltf/quantized` reads `KHR_mesh_quantization`: integer POSITION (signed or unsigned, 8 or 16 bit,
normalized or not) and normalized signed 8 or 16 bit NORMAL. Optimizers such as gltfpack write these. Values turn into
floats on load, so the file is smaller on the wire and the same size on the GPU.

```ts
import { Engine } from 'margoengine/core';
import { loadGLTF } from 'margoengine/gltf';
import { quantized } from 'margoengine/gltf/quantized';

const canvas = document.querySelector<HTMLCanvasElement>('canvas')!;
const engine = await Engine.create(canvas);
const model = await loadGLTF(engine, '/packed.glb', { extensions: [quantized] });
engine.start();
// On teardown: model.dispose(); engine.dispose();
```

### Base colour maps and cut-outs

`@margoengine/gltf/textured` draws `baseColorTexture` and `alphaMode: 'MASK'`, so a prop with one texture stays on the
light path. It reads any `TEXCOORD_n` set, in float or normalized form, applies `KHR_texture_transform`, multiplies by
`baseColorFactor` and cuts at `alphaCutoff` (default 0.5). PNG and JPEG images come from the GLB, a data URI or a URL
next to the file. Other maps, `BLEND`, and compressed or WebP textures still need `@margoengine/gltf-pro`.

```ts
import { Engine } from 'margoengine/core';
import { loadGLTF } from 'margoengine/gltf';
import { textured } from 'margoengine/gltf/textured';

const canvas = document.querySelector<HTMLCanvasElement>('canvas')!;
const engine = await Engine.create(canvas);
const model = await loadGLTF(engine, '/prop.glb', { extensions: [textured] });
engine.start();
// On teardown: model.dispose(); engine.dispose();
```

Images decode asynchronously, so for bytes already in memory use `parseGLTFAsync(engine, bytes, [], { extensions })` in
place of `parseGLTF`. WebGPU only: a WebGL engine refuses the file. The meshes stay core meshes, so they move, pick and
dispose as usual, and packages that patch core's shader apply to them. A cut-out casts its outline through
`@margoengine/shadows`, and `engine.stats.drawCalls` counts these draws. GPU picks see a cut-out as solid, because core's
pick draw has no uv; for a ray that passes through the holes, `texturedAlphaMasks(model, {signal, pixels})` gives
`AlphaRaycaster` its masks. Call it before `model.dispose()`; it reads each image once through an `OffscreenCanvas`, so in
Node pass `pixels`.

```ts
import { Engine } from 'margoengine/core';
import { AlphaRaycaster } from 'margoengine/bvh/alpha';
import { loadGLTF } from 'margoengine/gltf';
import { textured, texturedAlphaMasks } from 'margoengine/gltf/textured';

const engine = await Engine.create(document.querySelector('canvas')!);
const model = await loadGLTF(engine, '/fence.glb', { extensions: [textured] });
const ray = new AlphaRaycaster();
ray.alphaMask = await texturedAlphaMasks(model);
ray.firstHitOnly = true; // the nearest solid hit
ray.setFromEngine(engine, 320, 240);
console.log(ray.intersectEngine(engine)[0]?.mesh);
```

### Meshopt compression

`@margoengine/gltf/meshopt` reads `EXT_meshopt_compression` and `KHR_meshopt_compression`, every mode and filter.
`@margoengine/decoders/meshopt` is imported on the first file that uses them, so install `@margoengine/decoders` beside
this package; a file with no compressed views never loads it. A fallback buffer is not downloaded. Optimizers usually
quantize as well, so pass both.

```ts
import { Engine } from 'margoengine/core';
import { loadGLTF } from 'margoengine/gltf';
import { meshopt } from 'margoengine/gltf/meshopt';
import { quantized } from 'margoengine/gltf/quantized';
```

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/gltf.md]

=== @margoengine/gltf-pro (packages/gltf-pro/README.md) ===

# Margo Engine glTF Pro

Import `margoengine/gltf-pro` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/gltf-pro` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

`Picking.attach(engine)` from `@margoengine/selection` discovers loader-owned
primitive nodes automatically. `selection.set([primitive.node])` also discovers
their model; explicit `add(model)` remains supported and is deduplicated.
Custom buffer providers still register explicitly. Both consume `model.pickingPrimitives`,
which borrows the current static or GPU-deformed buffers and alpha metadata.
Registration changes no beauty shader, vertex layout or material bindings.

`model.readPickingGeometry()` returns an asynchronous, independently owned CPU
snapshot for `Raycaster.intersectModel(model)` in `@margoengine/bvh`. Static
geometry uses CPU copies; animated geometry is copied from the actual GPU output.
The optional `prepareDeformation` hook encodes the latest pose before reading,
without advancing animation time. Snapshots include world matrices, indices,
material sides and identity (`primitiveIndex` in `model.primitives`, absent for
point and line primitives, and the glTF `nodeIndex` when it has one) captured
with the query,
before any readback. Restoration, disposal or replacement of
an in-flight deformation output invalidates the result and releases staging
buffers. Caller-provided deformation buffers need `COPY_SRC` for CPU snapshots.

Use `import {GLTFAsset} from '@margoengine/gltf-pro/asset'` for accessor decoding
without loading PBR rendering or its shaders. The root export retains the same
constructor; `GLTFDocument` is available as a type from either entry.
`@margoengine/gltf-pro/splats` exports `gaussianSplats` and `readGaussianSplats` ([below](#gaussian-splats-in-gltf-splats)).
`@margoengine/gltf-pro/coordinates` exports `textureCoordinates` and the `TextureTransform` type (also on the root)
for material extensions that read texture coordinates without loading the renderer.

Optional WebGPU glTF 2.0 metallic-roughness rendering, separate from the frozen core and stage. The public npm name follows this repository's scope: `@margoengine/gltf-pro`.

Core + stage must remain below **25,000 bytes gzip**; CI rejects 25,000 bytes and above. Optional loaders, decoder code, workers and Wasm stay outside that measurement.

```ts
import {createStage} from 'margoengine';
import {loadGLTF, type MaterialExtension} from 'margoengine/gltf-pro';
const stage = await createStage('#viewport', {backend:'webgpu'});
const model = await loadGLTF(stage.engine, '/SciFiHelmet.glb');
const b = model.bounds;
stage.engine.camera.fitToBoundingBox([b[0],b[1],b[2]], [b[3],b[4],b[5]]);
// Call model.destroy() when unloading the model, or stage.dispose() on unmount.
```

`KHR_node_visibility` sets each node's `visible` flag, also when the extension is required. A hidden ancestor hides the meshes and lights below it; transforms, animation, sockets and cameras keep working. Toggle `model.nodes[index].visible` to change it. `model.clusteredLights()` leaves out lights under hidden nodes. After changing visibility, call `applyGLTFLights(model)` again to refresh the imported sun; if the model no longer has a visible sun, the lighting from before goes back, unless the caller changed it since. `@margoengine/animation/pointer` plays animated visibility (`KHR_animation_pointer`).

Supports base color/alpha, metallic-roughness (G/B), normal maps, occlusion (R), emissive, vertex colors, UV sets 0 to 3, tangents or derivative tangent frames, alpha masking/blending, double-sided materials, GLB/external buffers/images, normalized and sparse accessors. GGX, Smith, and Schlick implement analytical direct lighting with hemispherical ambient fill. Canvas output uses Khronos PBR Neutral tone mapping and sRGB encoding; HDR captures remain linear. Color/emissive textures decode sRGB; other maps remain linear. Images have generated mip chains and honor glTF filtering and wrapping.

The outside-reference test renders all 123 primitives of Khronos MetalRoughSpheresNoTextures with a shared
camera and sun. Against a Sample Viewer PNG, full-frame RGB byte MAE is 1.837511698404948 on the recorded
RTX A6000; the WebGL2 compatibility layer measures 1.837506612141927. Native WebGL2 rejects PBR with code
`unsupported`. These are measured error ceilings, not visual parity. The unresolved picture loss, full
settings, source hashes and coverage are in [batch 160 reproduction](../../docs/whitepaper/reproduce.md#batch-160-metallic-roughness).
From a built checkout, with the outside reference PNG already captured:

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/gltf-pro.md]

=== @margoengine/loaders (packages/loaders/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/loaders

Import `margoengine/loaders` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/loaders` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

PLY, STL, 3MF, DXF, PCD, OFF, XYZ, OBJ/MTL, COLLADA, Tiled TMX, legacy VTK and static USDA/USDZ loaders for Margo Engine, each tree-shakable on its own, plus three optional entries: TrueType fonts and extruded 3D text (`@margoengine/loaders/font`), SVG (`@margoengine/loaders/svg`) and OBJ meshes with their MTL materials and textures (`@margoengine/loaders/mtl`).

Packages that read their own formats import the shared parts without the other parsers: `@margoengine/loaders/common`
(`LoaderError`, `fetchBytes`, `readZipDirectory`, `readZipEntry`, `crc32`, `computeVertexNormals`, `faceNormal` and
the shared types) and `@margoengine/loaders/usd` (`parseUSDA`, `parseUSDZ`, `readUSDA`). Both are also on the root.

Build from source with `npm run build` in `packages/loaders`.

```ts
import {Engine} from 'margoengine/core';
import {load, parse3MF, parsePLY, createMeshes, toGeometry} from 'margoengine/loaders';
import {createMesh} from 'margoengine/materials';
import {box} from 'margoengine/core';
const signal = AbortSignal.timeout(30_000);
const canvas = document.querySelector('canvas')!;

const engine = await Engine.create(canvas);
const mesh = engine.createMesh().setGeometry(box());

// Fetch with a size limit and an AbortSignal, then parse. Limits go to the parser too.
const model = await load('/parts/bracket.3mf', parse3MF, {signal, maxBytes: 64 << 20, maxTriangles: 2_000_000});
const {meshes, dispose} = createMeshes(engine, model);   // one mesh + PbrMaterial per object color

// Or parse bytes you already have and build a core Geometry yourself.
const file = await fetch('/scans/part.ply');
const scan = parsePLY(await file.arrayBuffer());
mesh.setGeometry(toGeometry(scan, {normals: 'smooth'}));
```

Every parser returns the same `LoadedGeometry`:

```text
{kind: 'mesh' | 'points', positions: Float32Array, normals?, colors? /* sRGB 0..1 */, uvs?, indices?: Uint32Array,
 groups?: {start, count, name?, objectId?, color?: [r, g, b, a]}[], attributes?: Record<string, Float32Array>}
```

| Function | Reads |
| --- | --- |
| `parsePLY` | ASCII, binary little and big endian; x y z, nx ny nz, red green blue (uchar, ushort or float), s/t, u/v, texture_u/texture_v; polygon faces fan-triangulated; files without faces become point clouds; unknown elements and properties skipped |
| `parseSTL` | See [STL](#stl) |
| `parse3MF` (async) | Own ZIP reader (stored and deflate through `DecompressionStream('deflate-raw')`, CRC-32 checked); objects, meshes, components, build items, 3x4 transforms; `basematerials` and materials-extension `colorgroup` colors; production-extension `p:path` parts; unit conversion to meters |
| `parseDXF` | ASCII and binary DXF, every version: `$INSUNITS` to meters, LAYER colours and off/frozen layers, ACI and true colours (BYLAYER, BYBLOCK), blocks through INSERT (scale, rotation, rows and columns, nested) and DIMENSION; faces from 3DFACE, SOLID, TRACE, polyface and polygon-mesh POLYLINEs and MESH; line segments from LINE, LWPOLYLINE and 2D/3D POLYLINE (bulge arcs), ARC, CIRCLE, ELLIPSE and SPLINE (NURBS), in each entity's object coordinate system; POINT, TEXT and MTEXT (formatting removed); 3DSOLID, BODY and REGION ACIS data decoded to SAT text. Returns `{mesh, lines, points, texts, layers, solids, unit, version, skipped}`; draw `lines` with `@margoengine/lines` (`mode: 'segments'`) and the mesh double-sided (DXF faces have no winding) |
| `parsePCD` | `DATA ascii`, `binary`, `binary_compressed` (own LZF decompressor); x y z, normal_x/y/z, packed `rgb`/`rgba`, `intensity`, any other field skipped |
| `parseOFF` | `OFF` with `ST`, `C`, `N` prefixes (texture coordinates, colors 0..1 or 0..255, normals) |
| `parseXYZ` | xyz, xyz+rgb, xyz+normal, xyz+normal+rgb, xyz+intensity, PTS (xyz+intensity+rgb), chemistry XYZ |
| `parseVTK` | `# vtk DataFile Version` 1.0 to 5.1, ASCII or BINARY `DATASET POLYDATA`: POINTS, POLYGONS, TRIANGLE_STRIPS, 5.x OFFSETS/CONNECTIVITY, point NORMALS, COLOR_SCALARS, TEXTURE_COORDINATES, SCALARS |
| `parseOBJ` (async), `parseMTL` | See [OBJ and MTL](#obj-and-mtl) |
| `parseDAE`, `flattenDAE` | See [COLLADA](#collada) |

| `parseVRML`, `parseX3D` (`/vrml`) | See [VRML and X3D](#vrml-and-x3d) |

=== @margoengine/decoders (packages/decoders/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/decoders

Import `margoengine/decoders` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/decoders` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

Worker-pooled Draco geometry decoding, KTX2/Basis Universal texture transcoding and EXT_meshopt_compression decoding, and synchronous PNG, TGA, PCX, TIFF, DDS and KTX 1 reading (`@margoengine/decoders/png`, `/tga`, `/tiff`, `/dds`, `/ktx`), for Margo Engine.

Build from source with `npm run build` in `packages/decoders`.

```ts
import {DracoDecoder, KTX2Decoder} from 'margoengine/decoders';
import {Engine} from 'margoengine/core';
const engine = await Engine.create(document.querySelector('canvas')!);
const bytes = new Uint8Array(await (await fetch('/mesh.drc')).arrayBuffer());

const draco = new DracoDecoder({workerLimit: 4});
const ktx2 = new KTX2Decoder({device: engine.gpu!, workerLimit: 4});

// A KHR_draco_mesh_compression bufferView, with the extension's attribute ids.
const geometry = await draco.decode(bytes, {attributeIds: {POSITION: 0, NORMAL: 1, TEXCOORD_0: 2}});
geometry.positions; // Float32Array
geometry.indices;   // Uint16Array or Uint32Array

// Transcodes to BC7, ASTC 4x4, ETC2 or RGBA8, whichever the device has enabled, then writes every mip level.
const texture = await ktx2.createTexture(await (await fetch('/albedo.ktx2')).arrayBuffer());

// On teardown:
draco.dispose(); ktx2.dispose();
```

A standalone `.ktx2` goes on a material map through `@margoengine/materials`: `loadKTX2Texture(url, {decoder: ktx2})`,
or `new Texture(await ktx2.transcode(bytes))`, which uploads the transcoded mips on each device that draws it.

## Meshopt

`decodeMeshoptBuffer(source, count, stride, mode, filter)` decodes one `EXT_meshopt_compression` or `KHR_meshopt_compression` bufferView (ATTRIBUTES, TRIANGLES or INDICES, with the OCTAHEDRAL, QUATERNION, EXPONENTIAL and COLOR filters) and returns a `Uint8Array`. It is pure TypeScript, written from the two extension specifications, synchronous and needs no Wasm. Output matches the meshoptimizer reference decoder bit for bit. Attribute streams of vertex codec version 0 (the only one `EXT_meshopt_compression` defines) and version 1 (added by `KHR_meshopt_compression`) are both decoded, whichever extension names the bufferView; any other version is rejected with a clear error. `MeshoptDecoder` has the members of the meshoptimizer project's own decoder object (`supported`, `ready`, `decodeGltfBuffer`), so glTF loaders written against that interface work unchanged.

## Meshopt on Wasm SIMD (`@margoengine/decoders/meshopt-simd`)

`meshoptDecodeGltfBufferSIMD` takes the arguments of `meshoptDecodeGltfBuffer` and gives the same bytes and the same errors, on a
25 KB Wasm module built from `native/meshopt-simd` in this package. It is embedded in the entry, so importing it costs nothing
elsewhere and nobody who installs the package needs Rust. Until `ready` resolves, on a runtime without Wasm SIMD, and on any
stream the module will not read, the TypeScript decoder runs instead.

```ts
import {MeshoptSIMDDecoder, meshoptDecodeGltfBufferSIMD} from 'margoengine/decoders/meshopt-simd';
const bytes = new Uint8Array(await (await fetch('/meshopt.bin')).arrayBuffer());

await MeshoptSIMDDecoder.ready;
const positions = meshoptDecodeGltfBufferSIMD(bytes, 1000, 12, 'ATTRIBUTES');
```

`MeshoptSIMDDecoder` has the members of `MeshoptDecoder` (`supported`, `ready`, `decodeGltfBuffer`), so a loader written against
that interface can take either. After changing the Rust source run `node scripts/meshopt-simd-build.mjs`; a test fails while the
embedded module and the source differ. To time both decoders on a file: `node scripts/meshopt-simd-bench.mjs <file.glb>`.

## JPEG XL (`@margoengine/decoders/jxl`)

`JXLDecoder` decodes `.jxl` files to RGBA8: straight alpha, sRGB, top row first. A browser that reads JPEG XL does the work; anywhere
else a module worker loads a Wasm build of jxl-oxide on the first decode, so importing the entry downloads no Wasm until a file
needs it. `jxlTextureFile` turns the result into a `TextureFile`.

```ts
import {JXLDecoder, jxlTextureFile, uploadTexture} from 'margoengine/decoders/jxl';
const device = await (await navigator.gpu.requestAdapter())!.requestDevice();
const file = await (await fetch('/texture.jxl')).arrayBuffer();

using decoder = new JXLDecoder();
const image = await decoder.decode(file);
const texture = uploadTexture(device, jxlTextureFile(image));
```

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/decoders.md]

=== @margoengine/fbx (packages/fbx/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/fbx

Import `margoengine/fbx` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/fbx` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

Native binary and ASCII FBX import through Margo's first-party glTF exporter and optional PBR/animation pipeline. Core, stage, and the animation runtime are unchanged.

```ts
import {loadFBX} from 'margoengine/fbx';
import {Animation} from 'margoengine/animation';
import {Engine} from 'margoengine/core';
const engine = await Engine.create(document.querySelector('canvas')!);
const model = await loadFBX(engine, '/assets/character.fbx');
const animation = Animation.attach(model);
animation.play('Walking');
```

`convertFBX(bytes, options)` returns a GLB `ArrayBuffer`. `parseFBX(engine, bytes, options)` returns a `PBRModel`. `loadFBX(engine, stringOrURL, options)` fetches an HTTP(S) asset and resolves texture paths against the final response URL. Options remain `{resourcePath?: string; signal?: AbortSignal}`. Explicit resource paths must use HTTP(S).

## Supported first implementation

- A connection naming an object the file left out is dropped: the FBX SDK writes such links, for curves on properties a plug-in owns.
- Binary FBX versions 7100-7700 with 32/64-bit node records, raw arrays, and zlib-compressed arrays. Array headers remain 32-bit in every supported version. ASCII uses the same scene conversion.
- Bounded concave triangulation; normal, UV, tangent/binormal, color, and material layers with Direct/IndexToDirect and ByControlPoint/ByVertice/ByPolygonVertex/ByPolygon/AllSame mappings. The first attribute layer and UV set are imported, or up to four UV sets and two colour layers with the `layers` option; UV V and tangent handedness convert to glTF conventions.
- Area-weighted normals, UV/hard-edge vertex splitting, shared geometry instances, and material partitions. Multiple material partitions become separate child mesh nodes under the original model transform.
- Six fixed-axis Euler orders, pivots/offsets, pre-rotation and inverse post-rotation, mesh-only geometric transforms, units, and signed axis conversion. Missing GlobalSettings preserves raw coordinates. Canonical FBX Y-up uses FrontAxisSign +1; Blender Z-up converts `(x,y,z)` to `(x,z,-y)`.
- Linear Normalize skin clusters, exact joint IDs and bind matrices, four strongest influences with deterministic tie order and normalization, and remapping onto split vertices.
- Single-shape blend channels with sparse position/normal deltas, names, initial weights, and animated percent weights. Blender's all-100 per-control-point FullWeights convention is accepted.
- Lambert/Phong dielectric materials, diffuse/emissive colors, opacity/transparency, shininess-derived roughness, and embedded or external PNG/JPEG diffuse and normal textures. Emission above 1 goes to `KHR_materials_emissive_strength`. An image the server answers 404 or 410 for, or in another format, is left off and named in the material's `extras.fbxMissingTextures`; the model still comes. A full path from the writer's PC is looked for by its file name beside the FBX.
- What real files hold and tools keep: a polygon with a corner repeated (skipped), no area (no triangles) or crossing itself (drawn from its corners); a UV index of -1 (that corner sits at the origin); a joint cluster with no lists; weights for control points the mesh lost after binding (dropped). A file of a skeleton and curves alone, such as Unity's `Name@Clip.fbx`, converts with `convertFBX`; `parseFBX` needs a mesh.
- Multiple animation stacks, one layer per stack (any number with `animationLayers`), STEP and LINEAR curves (every kind with `animationLayers`), missing-axis rest values, and interpolation at common key times. LINEAR transform tracks are adaptively baked for Euler motion and moving pivots, with sampled translation/scale tolerance `1e-5 * max(1, magnitude)` and angular tolerance `1e-4` radians. These are sampling criteria, not a proof of continuous error bounds. Rotation segments are subdivided to preserve full turns.

## UV sets and colour layers

`layers: true` keeps up to four UV sets and two colour layers instead of the first of each, for lightmaps and detail textures. They arrive as `TEXCOORD_0` to `TEXCOORD_3` and `COLOR_0`, `COLOR_1`, in the file's layer order.

```ts
import {loadFBX} from 'margoengine/fbx';
import {Engine} from 'margoengine/core';
const engine = await Engine.create(document.querySelector('canvas')!);
const model = await loadFBX(engine, '/assets/room.fbx', {layers: true});
console.log(model.primitives.length);
```

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/fbx.md]

=== @margoengine/usdz (packages/usdz/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/usdz

Import `margoengine/usdz` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/usdz` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

Optional static USDA, USDC and USDZ ingestion into `@margoengine/gltf-pro`. Core and the stage facade are unchanged. The package uses Margo's shared bounded USDA tokenizer and ZIP reader, plus its native Crate decoder for USDC. Building and using it requires no external renderer or CAD runtime.

USDZ remains an ancillary format outside the six core launch packages and is not a core launch blocker.

```ts
import {Engine} from 'margoengine/core';
import {loadUSDZ} from 'margoengine/usdz';

const canvas=document.createElement('canvas');document.body.append(canvas);
const engine=await Engine.create(canvas,{backend:'webgpu',capacity:10000});
const model=await loadUSDZ(engine,'/model.usdz');
engine.start();
// model.destroy() detaches its PBR plugin and frees meshes/textures.
```

For the executable README check, `/model.usdz` maps to Needle's published Blender 5.1 conversion
of Cesium's BoxTextured sample (CC-BY-4.0 with trademark limitations). Run
`node scripts/fetch-readme-assets.mjs` from the repository root to fetch its hash-checked USDZ into
the shared external cache. The example exercises the static reader, including its archived texture;
it does not require an animation or subdivision extension.

`parseUSDA(textOrBytes)`, `parseUSDC(bytes)`, and async `parseUSDZ(bytes)` return a `USDAsset` with typed mesh streams, a glTF document/buffers, and async `create(engine)` to attach PBR rendering. `loadUSDZ` fetches with streaming byte bounds and creates the model. Malformed, unsupported or oversized input throws a `LoaderError` (`error.format === 'USD'`; `error.code` is `syntax`, `unsupported` or `limit`). Options: `maxBytes`, `maxVertices`, `maxTriangles`, `maxDepth`, `signal`. Defaults: 64 MiB, one million expanded vertices/triangles, depth 32. The engine grows its store when the hierarchy plus the PBR model root exceed the initial capacity. Texture ownership passes to the PBR model and is released on destruction or failed setup.

Supports stored and Deflate ZIP entries with CRC checks, static ASCII/binary hierarchies, Y/Z up and authored units, ordered translate/scale/rotateXYZ/affine transforms, triangles and convex planar polygons, left-handed winding, authored normals and vertex/face-varying UVs including indices, inherited material bindings, and constant UsdPreviewSurface diffuse/roughness/metallic factors. UsdUVTexture diffuse and normal maps are decoded from the archive. A texture's `wrapS`/`wrapT` (`repeat`, `mirror`, `clamp`; `black` and `useMetadata` fall back to repeat) become a glTF sampler, and a `UsdTransform2d` on its `st` becomes `KHR_texture_transform` (same angle and sign, in radians). `mesh.uvs` holds `st` as authored (origin at the image's bottom left); the glTF document holds them as uvs (s, 1 - t). Separate roughness and metallic maps are packed into glTF's green/blue channels during creation.

Standard USDZ is an uncompressed, aligned archive. Deflate support accepts a broader ZIP envelope for interoperability. Stored entries reuse archive views. Decompression, Crate decoding, topology expansion, texture packing and GPU upload require allocations: this is **not** end-to-end zero-copy. Geometry conversion writes flat typed arrays without allocating an object per output vertex; metadata and hierarchy objects remain necessary.

Vertex colors read through a `UsdPrimvarReader` of `displayColor` or `displayOpacity` load as `mesh.colors` (four floats per vertex) and glTF COLOR_0, a constant `inputs:opacity` or the base colour map's alpha gives `BLEND`, or `MASK` with `inputs:opacityThreshold`; so a file from `exportUSDZ` keeps its paint and alpha. A separate opacity map and a reader of any other primvar are refused.

Without the entries below this is a static mesh subset of one flattened layer: meshes need `subdivisionScheme = "none"`, and subdivision or hole faces are refused. A prim may reference a class or other prim of the same layer (`references = </Path>`, what `exportUSDZ` writes for a shared geometry), and what it authors wins; class prims are not drawn. Other composition is refused. A mesh's `GeomSubset`s with materials are primitives of their own (`mesh.subsets`), a texture reads the primvar its `UsdPrimvarReader` names, every `xformOp` of the schema is read (`rotateX`, all six Euler orders, `orient`, suffixes such as `xformOp:translate:pivot` and `!invert!`), `!resetXformStack!` is honoured (see [Reset transform stacks](#reset-transform-stacks)), guide and proxy meshes are left out, and a mesh with no material shows its `displayColor`. Physical Apple AR Quick Look round trips are untested.

## Composition
