=== @margoengine/voxel-edit (packages/voxel-edit/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/voxel-edit

Import `margoengine/voxel-edit` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/voxel-edit` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

Editing voxel models for voxel editors and tools: dense and sparse grids, modeling operations, brushes and
selections, picking, export meshing, `.vox` scene editing and frame animation. CPU only (but `./shaders` and `./gpu`, which run on a GPUDevice), no renderer, no DOM: every
function is pure and can run in a worker. Optional and tree-shakable; core and the stage never import it.

```ts
import { combineGrids, mergePalettes, rotateGrid, type VoxelGrid } from 'margoengine/voxel-edit';
import { sphereCells, connectedCells } from 'margoengine/voxel-edit/edit';
import { pickRay, raycastGrid } from 'margoengine/voxel-edit/pick';
import { meshGrid } from 'margoengine/voxel-edit/mesh';
import {Engine} from 'margoengine/core';
const ndcX = 0;
const ndcY = 0;
const engine = await Engine.create(document.querySelector('canvas')!);

const model: VoxelGrid = { size: [32, 32, 32], voxels: new Uint8Array(32 * 32 * 32) };
const { grid } = rotateGrid(model, { axis: 'y', degrees: 90 }); // a new grid; `model` is unchanged
const prop: VoxelGrid = { size: [8, 8, 8], voxels: new Uint8Array(8 * 8 * 8) };
const baseKeys = Array.from({ length: 256 }, (_, i) => `base:${i}`), toolKeys = Array.from({ length: 256 }, (_, i) => `tool:${i}`);
const baseUsed = new Uint8Array(256), toolUsed = new Uint8Array(256);
const { paletteMap } = mergePalettes({ baseKeys, toolKeys, baseUsed, toolUsed });
const merged = combineGrids(grid, prop, { operation: 'union', offset: [4, 0, 4], paletteMap });

const ray = pickRay(engine.camera.matrix, ndcX, ndcY); // then into the model's cells with its inverse matrix
const hit = ray && raycastGrid(merged.grid, ray); // {cell, adjacent, normal, value, distance}
const { mesh } = meshGrid(merged.grid, { ambientOcclusion: true, pivot: [16, 0, 16] });
```

## Grids

A `VoxelGrid` is `{size, voxels}`: one palette index per cell, 0 for air and 1-255 for filled cells, Y up, cell
(x, y, z) at `x + size[0] * (z + size[2] * y)` (`cellIndex`, `cellAt`, `insideGrid`). Operations never change their
input; each returns `{grid, changed, clipped}`: a new grid, the cells that differ (cells outside either grid read as
air) and the filled cells pushed out of bounds. Every operation checks its arguments and its `maxCells` budget
(default 16,777,216 cells, at most 67,108,864) before allocating anything. The layout operations (`flipGrid` to
`fitGrid`) also take a `selection` of cell indexes and return it mapped, with `mapPoint` for pivots and joints in
corner coordinates.

| Root entry | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `combineGrids` | union (with a `paletteMap`), `intersect`, `subtract` of a tool grid at a whole-cell offset |
| `mergePalettes` | the `paletteMap` for a union: reuses equal identities, takes free indexes, never changes used base entries; throws past 255 |
| `shearGrid`, `reflectDiagonal`, `wrapGrid`, `rotateGrid` | shear by layers, mirror or symmetrize across a square plane's diagonal, move with wrap-around, turn by any angle inside the box |
| `repeatGrid`, `resampleGrid` | tile, or scale by nearest-cell sampling (indexes are never blended) |
| `dilateGrid`, `erodeGrid`, `fillEnclosed` | grow or shrink along chosen axis directions, fill closed cavities |
| `generateMaze` | a seeded perfect maze, one-cell walls and corridors |
| `flipGrid`, `turnGrid`, `shiftGrid` | exact whole-cell layout: mirror along a principal axis, right-handed quarter turns that swap the other two sizes (so nothing clips; `rotateGrid` turns inside the same box instead), move by an offset with the cells that leave counted in `clipped` |
| `occupiedBounds`, `cropGrid`, `fitGrid` | the filled box; crop or extend to a size anchored at a caller's origin (a resize keeping the corner is origin [0, 0, 0]); shrink to the filled box |
| `invertGrid` | swap filled and empty cells, air taking an explicit palette index |
| `sliceLayout`, `stackSlices` | sprite-sheet RGBA frames (explicit frame size, columns, count, stack axis, order and alpha threshold) stacked into an indexed Y-up grid, each RGBA colour exact: indexes in reading order up to 255, or the first exact index of a palette you pass; anything else refuses |
| `ByteLedger`, `ownedBuffers`, `retainedBytes` | bytes of the storage grids, cels, packed frames, images and sparse snapshots keep alive, each buffer counted once through its token (`SparseGrid.ownedBuffers`, `SparseGrid.deltaBuffers`); the ledger retains and releases values for an undo budget |

## Entries

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/voxel-edit.md]

=== @margoengine/water (packages/water/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/water

Import `margoengine/water` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/water` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

A separate WebGPU water grid evaluates up to eight swell trains with analytical normals. Each train spreads into three Gerstner components with varied directions, wavelengths and gently bending crests. Advected gradient noise (random unit gradients, Perlin's 2002 quintic fade, analytic derivatives) adds wind agitation and micro-ripples, filtered separately by their screen footprint. Fresnel reflection, sun glints and wavelength-dependent absorption shade the surface. Optional terrain coupling adds conservative GPU shallow-water flow, moving breaker foam and a fixed GPU spray pool.

```ts
import {Water} from 'margoengine/water';
import {Engine} from 'margoengine/core';
const engine = await Engine.create(document.querySelector('canvas')!);
const water = Water.attach(engine, {size: [100,100], segments: 128, height: 0});
```

For an open ocean, set `horizon: true`. The central 75% of each grid axis keeps
its original spacing and follows the camera in whole cells, so the swell
surrounds the camera wherever it goes and the waves stay put in the world. Each
outer row is a fixed ratio wider than the one inside it, out to 10 km past the
grid's edge, and the last row lies 10,000 km out, so the sea meets the true
horizon even from a camera kilometres up; both draw beyond the scene's far clip.
Wave displacement and normals fade
together over those rows as the cells grow too large to resolve the wavelength.
The default grid remains bounded and centred on the origin for ponds and finite
surfaces. Use a size that keeps the shoreline and terrain map within 37.5% of
`size` of the camera, where the cells are regular.

```ts
import {Bloom} from 'margoengine/post/bloom';
import {Sky} from 'margoengine/sky';
import {Water} from 'margoengine/water';
import {Engine} from 'margoengine/core';
const engine = await Engine.create(document.querySelector('canvas')!);
// A 4 km sea on 8 m cells: the swell follows the camera to the horizon.
const sea = Water.attach(engine, {
  size: [4096, 4096],
  segments: 512,
  horizon: true,
  waves: [{direction: [1, 0.3], amplitude: 0.9, wavelength: 48}],
});
```

Directions are XZ, dimensions/amplitudes are world units, wavelengths are positive, and phase is radians. A configured wave supplies the dominant direction and wavelength of its train; its three component amplitudes sum to the configured amplitude. Invalid steepness that would fold the surface is rejected. The crest bend includes analytical derivatives and a displacement margin to preserve that bound. Agitation and micro-ripples follow the first wave's direction; each of their four layers is turned by its own angle (11° to 41°) and scaled by non-integer ratios, so no two noise lattices line up into visible streaks. Open-water sky reflections clamp below-horizon rays to the horizon and soften with roughness. Fresnel inputs are saturated before exponentiation so floating-point roundoff cannot feed a negative base into `pow`. Default water owns a shared sampleable scene-depth target with HTML. With Bloom/SSAO/DOF, pass `depth: () => effect.depthTexture` explicitly; dimensions must match the viewport. Water is opaque and Y-up. It seeds its own depth target from opaque scene depth and writes that target to resolve overlapping wave triangles; the original scene depth stays available for shoreline comparisons. Default foam history is screen-space and resets on resize/restoration. Each engine view keeps its own foam history; a view not drawn for a frame releases it.

For the sandbox optics, connect the optional packages:

```ts
const bloom = Bloom.attach(engine), sky = Sky.attach(engine);
Water.attach(engine, {
  depth: () => bloom.depthTexture,
  sceneColor: () => bloom.sceneTexture,
  reflection: () => sky.reflectionTexture,
  lights: sky.lights,
});
```

The borrowed sky texture must be a sampleable single-layer `rgba16float` 2D texture. The borrowed scene color must be a viewport-sized single-layer `rgba16float` texture with `COPY_SRC` usage. Water retains one GPU snapshot for depth-rejected screen refraction and seabed attenuation. Without these providers, it uses a sky gradient and an approximate seabed color. Reflections represent the atmosphere, not nearby objects.

`water.depthTexture` exposes borrowed viewport depth including opaque geometry and
the water surface for subsequent effects, such as `Sky` distance fog. It is
undefined before the first draw and after disposal/restoration until drawing
resumes. Its 1x/4x sample count follows scene quality, and the texture changes on
resize or device restoration. Consumers must re-read it and must not destroy it.

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/water.md]

=== @margoengine/scenery (packages/scenery/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/scenery

Import `margoengine/scenery` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/scenery` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

A moonlit night sky for Margo Engine: twinkling stars, a phased moon with glow, and horizon haze. `SkyMoon` is a
preset of `Sky` from `@margoengine/sky` (Margo's one sky implementation) held at midnight with its stylized
`night` options. `addSky(stage)` (`@margoengine/stage/sky`) loads it.

In this workspace, `npm run modern:dev` opens the starter; click **Toggle moonlit scenery**.

Once the packages are on npm (not yet; build from source until then):

```sh
npm install @margoengine/core @margoengine/scenery
```

```ts
import {Engine} from 'margoengine/core';

const canvas = document.querySelector<HTMLCanvasElement>('canvas')!;
const engine = await Engine.create(canvas, {backend: 'webgpu'});
const {SkyMoon} = await import('margoengine/scenery/sky');
const sky = SkyMoon.attach(engine, {moonDirection: [0.45, 0, -1], moonPhase: 0.85});
engine.start();
sky.config.moonPhase = 0.2; // read every frame
```

`@margoengine/scenery/sky` and the root export `SkyMoon` and the `SkyMoonConfig` type (an alias of Sky's
`SkyNightOptions`). `SkyMoon.attach(engine, config)` is `engine.use(new SkyMoon(config))`, and `new SkyMoon(config)` is `new Sky({hours: 0, timeScale: 0, night: config}, {night})` from
`@margoengine/sky/base` with plugin name `sky-moon`: it loads only the stylized-night feature (about 6.6 kB min+gzip
summed over this entry, Sky's base and Sky's night, against 10.2 kB for the full Sky;
[entry-sizes.json](../../examples/package-benchmarks/results/entry-sizes.json)), so it is not an `instanceof` the root `Sky`, and options that need
other features (fog, clouds, a day model) throw; build a `Sky` with those features instead. `config` (also
`sky.options.night`) is read every frame, so change it in place for live controls. Remove it with
`engine.removePlugin('sky-moon')` or `sky.dispose()`.

The options, defaults and limits are Sky's stylized night (see the `@margoengine/sky` README): zenith and horizon
colours, `hazeDensity`, moon direction, angular size, phase, colour and glow, star intensity and twinkle. The sky
draws behind opaque geometry at reversed-Z depth 0, on canvas and HDR targets, with 1x or 4x sampling. Its
colours are written as given on both.

The low-level `SkyMoonPass` (`@margoengine/scenery/sky-moon`) and the Night Citadel's `NightAtmosphere` were
removed when the three sky implementations were merged into `@margoengine/sky`. Use `Sky` directly for custom
night skies, and Sky's `fog` (`falloff: 'exp'`, `height`, `color`) for the citadel's height haze.

## Day presets

`@margoengine/scenery/presets` holds four times of day, `noon`, `goldenHour`, `overcast` and `dawn`, as options for
`Sky` from `@margoengine/sky`, with the light that goes with each. The sun's colour and strength are not stored: the
sky works them out from its own air (`sunlight` in `@margoengine/sky`), so the light always matches the sky drawn.

```ts
import {Engine} from 'margoengine/core';
import {Sky} from 'margoengine/sky';
import {applyDayPreset, dayLight, dayPreset} from 'margoengine/scenery/presets';

const canvas = document.querySelector<HTMLCanvasElement>('canvas')!;
const engine = await Engine.create(canvas, {backend: 'webgpu'});
const sky = Sky.attach(engine, dayPreset('goldenHour'));
engine.start();
applyDayPreset(sky, 'overcast'); // switch a running sky
console.log(dayLight('noon').intensity); // the sun strength the sky drives into the engine light
```

- `dayPreset(name)` returns fresh `SkyOptions`: the sun placed by `sunDirection` with the clock held
  (`timeScale: 0`), `turbidity`, a cloud sheet when the preset has cloud, the backdrop `exposure`, and `lighting`
  with the direct sun strength overhead and a diffuse floor (`ambient.day`, and `[0.01, 0.015, 0.03]` by night). Use the
  root `Sky`, which has the clouds and lighting features these need. Pass a name or a `DayPreset` object.
- `applyDayPreset(sky, name)` writes a preset into a running sky's `options` (read every frame), removes a cloud sheet
  the preset has none of and keeps the rest (fog, night, model).
- `dayLight(name)` is the sun the sky drives on the first frame (`direction`, `color` with its largest channel 1,
  `intensity`) and the diffuse floor, for a scene that lights itself.
- `DAY_PRESETS` holds the frozen values and `dayPresetNames` the names. Copy one to make your own:
  `dayPreset({...DAY_PRESETS.noon, elevation: 50})`. Unknown names and out-of-range values throw `RangeError`.

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/scenery.md]

=== @margoengine/scatter (packages/scatter/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/scatter

Import `margoengine/scatter` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/scatter` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

`randomPlacements(count, bounds, [minScale,maxScale], seed)` generates seeded
rectangle candidates. `radialPlacements(centers, perCenter, [minDistance,maxDistance],
[minScale,maxScale], seed)` generates candidates around world XZ anchors. Both
produce `[x,z,scale,yaw]` tuples at initialization. Submit them to a shared
`PlacementLayout` to filter overlaps and reserve accepted footprints.

`instanceTransforms()` packs `[x,y,z,scale,yaw]` placements into affine matrices.
`groundTransforms(placements, height, offsetY)` accepts `[x,z,scale,yaw]`, samples
world height, and applies a vertical offset (negative values sink roots).
`placementBounds(placements,radius)` produces enclosing world XZ rectangles.
`clearPlacements(candidates,radius,exclusions,gap)` accepts rectangle exclusions
`[minX,minZ,maxX,maxZ]` and circle exclusions `[x,z,radius]`; the optional gap
defaults to 0. These initialization helpers preserve their inputs and validate
height samples, scales and exclusion data.

WebGPU seeded, stratified placement with density, world-height and slope rules. Compute culling packs instances into three distance LOD rings, followed by indexed indirect draws.

The rings keep candidate order: each frame they hold the same instances in the same order on every GPU, so a still
view draws the same pixels frame after frame, 4x MSAA edges included (an Apple M6 drew other edge pixels every frame
when the rings were filled with atomics). The cost is a slower cull pass and about 58 bytes of GPU memory per
candidate; [docs/limits.md](../../docs/limits.md) ("Scatter cull in candidate order") has the measured numbers.
`node packages/scatter/test/repeat.browser.mjs` checks repeated frames bit for bit.

```ts
import {Scatter} from 'margoengine/scatter';
import {sphereGeometry, toGeometry} from 'margoengine/geometry';
import {Engine} from 'margoengine/core';
const engine = await Engine.create(document.querySelector('canvas')!);
const nearGeometry = toGeometry(sphereGeometry(0.5, 16, 8)), midGeometry = toGeometry(sphereGeometry(0.5, 8, 4));
const farGeometry = toGeometry(sphereGeometry(0.5, 4, 2));
const scatter = Scatter.attach(engine, [nearGeometry, midGeometry, farGeometry], {
  count: 10000, area: [50,50], density: 0.8, maxSlope: 45, lod: [25,60,120], lodFade: 2
});
```

A single Geometry can be supplied for all rings; the package does not auto-decimate meshes. heightmap returns a sampleable red-channel height texture covering area around center, one height per texel centre (as `TerrainHeightmap` writes it). Each instance takes the bilinear interpolation of the four texel centres around it, and the ground normal (for `maxSlope`) is that patch's gradient, so roots follow slopes between texels. Heights are world units plus center Y; absent heightmap is flat. Rules are fixed at construction and distribution is evaluated on GPU each frame. Output uses random Y rotation and scale with a simple diffuse material. Three storage buffers reserve count instances each, so account for GPU memory; device limits are checked. No core geometry/material feature additions are needed.

The default LOD distances are `[25,60,120]` world units. All three distances must fit positive normal f32 values
(at least 2^-126 after conversion) and remain strictly increasing after GPU upload; values that collapse to zero
or equal boundaries are rejected with RangeError, including in ScatterTiles. `lodFade` defaults to a
2-unit overlap centered on each of the first two distances. Compute emits both
adjacent meshes inside that band; complementary 4x4 Bayer masks cross-fade them
in both diffuse and PBR rendering, without alpha blending or per-frame history.
The width is clamped to prevent overlapping bands. Identical adjacent Geometry
objects skip the extra draw instances. Set `lodFade: 0` for hard switches.
The third distance remains the culling boundary. `edgeShrink` (world units,
default 0) scales instances down to zero over that last stretch instead of
cutting them at it, so the far edge of a grass field recedes without popping;
it needs no fade mask or `discard`, so it also suits the phone tier.

`inner` (world units, default 0: off) leaves a hole round the camera, so another
layer can take over nearby, such as stored objects in front of far stand-ins.
`innerFade` (world units, default 0: a sharp circle) is a band past `inner` where
instances appear one by one, each at its own hashed distance. Both are measured in
3D like the LOD distances, and `inner` must be below the last one. Instances beyond
`inner + innerFade` are the very same ones as without the option, and without it the
distribute shader stays the same text.

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/scatter.md]

=== @margoengine/road (packages/road/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/road

Import `margoengine/road` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/road` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

Arc-length spline sweeps generate a road surface, raised curbs, hard cross-section normals and tiled UV coordinates.

```ts
import {road} from 'margoengine/road';
import {Spline} from 'margoengine/splines';
import {Engine} from 'margoengine/core';
const engine = await Engine.create(document.querySelector('canvas')!);
const curve = new Spline([[0, 0, 0], [40, 2, 30], [90, 0, 20]]);
const {geometry, uvs} = road(curve, {width: 6, curbWidth: 0.2, curbHeight: 0.15, uvMeters: 5});
engine.createMesh().setGeometry(geometry);
```

Custom crossSection entries are [lateralOffset, height]. UV V follows distance / uvMeters and U follows cross-section distance. The core is frozen and has no UV channel: uvs is separate data for a textured optional renderer/exporter. Sweeps are Y-up and reject vertical or zero tangents; banking and self-intersection repair are not included in the root sweep.

## Junctions

`@margoengine/road/junctions` stitches crossings and T junctions by uniting the entire road footprint before triangulation. Draw this returned surface instead of overlapping road sweeps. It also preserves courtyard holes. Geometry's existing polygon and triangulation entries load only when the function is called; the road root does not load them.

```ts
import {junctions} from 'margoengine/road/junctions';
import {Engine} from 'margoengine/core';
const engine = await Engine.create(document.querySelector('canvas')!);
const {geometry, area} = await junctions([
  {points: [[-10, 0], [10, 0]], width: 4},
  {points: [[0, -10], [0, 10]], width: 4},
]);
engine.createMesh().setGeometry(geometry);
console.log(area); // 144 square metres, not 160 with the crossing counted twice
```

Points are horizontal `[x, z]` metres. Each line has `width` (default 6). Options are `elevation` (default 0), `uvMeters` (default 1), and `signal` (default none). The signal is checked before and after lazy loading; synchronous geometry work cannot be interrupted. Inputs are snapshotted before loading. The result owns `geometry` and `uvs`, with world-space `[x, -z] / uvMeters`, and needs no disposal; dispose meshes and engines when finished.

Limits: 1..64 roads, 2..4096 points per line and 4096 total, no equal neighbours, coordinates/elevation within +/-1,000,000 m, widths in (0,1000], UV scale in (0,1,000,000]. Bevel joins and butt ends, a shared constant elevation, no curbs, turn-radius design or bridge separation. The polygon grid has about 2^26 steps across the footprint; features below two steps may vanish. Result geometry uses float32 coordinates, so place small roads near their local origin. Collapsed or reversed float32 triangles and overflowing UVs reject with coded help-linked errors. Both WebGPU and the WebGL2 compatibility layer render the same CPU-generated geometry. The GPU test checks road and clear pixels, exact restoration after device reboot, and mesh/engine disposal on both.

GPU tests from the repository root: `node scripts/gpu-lock.mjs run --owner=road-tests --max=8 --wait-max=10 -- npm run test:gpu --workspace @margoengine/road`.

Apache-2.0. Optional, tree-shakable package; core peer: ^0.1.0 || ^1.0.0.

Build and unit tests: npm test --workspace @margoengine/road

=== @margoengine/tilemap (packages/tilemap/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/tilemap

Import `margoengine/tilemap` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/tilemap` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

The 2D tile map format every other piece builds on: `TileMapData` holds the tile size, tilesets with per-tile properties, animation and collision shapes, tile layers as `Uint32Array` with Tiled's flip bits, object layers, parallax, offset, opacity and custom properties. The root entry has the types, small helpers and the `TileMap` renderer; auto-tiling and the Tiled importer are their own entries. `TileMap` draws orthogonal maps; `GridTileMap` of the `iso` entry draws isometric, staggered and hexagonal ones. (`@margoengine/tiles` is OGC 3D Tiles; this package is unrelated.)

```ts
import {createTileLayer, encodeTile, FLIP_H, tileAt, validateTileMap, type TileMapData} from 'margoengine/tilemap';
const ground = createTileLayer('ground', 2, 2, Uint32Array.of(1, encodeTile(2, FLIP_H), 0, 1));
const map: TileMapData = {
  width: 2, height: 2, tileWidth: 16, tileHeight: 16, layers: [ground],
  tilesets: [{name: 'grass', firstGid: 1, tileWidth: 16, tileHeight: 16, tileCount: 2, columns: 2,
    image: {source: 'grass.png', width: 32, height: 16}, tiles: [{id: 1, properties: {solid: true}}]}],
};
validateTileMap(map);
console.log(tileAt(ground, 1, 0)); // 2147483650: tile 2, mirrored left to right
```

Layer values keep the low 28 bits for the global tile id (0 is empty) and the top bits for `FLIP_H`, `FLIP_V` and `FLIP_D`, exactly as Tiled stores them, so imported data is used as is. `decodeTile` and `encodeTile` split and join them; `tilesetForGid` and `tileDefForGid` find the tileset and the per-tile entry; `validateTileMap` throws a `TypeError` or `RangeError` that names the field.

## Drawing a map

`TileMap` draws the tile layers with exact pixels: one instanced draw per visible 64 x 64 chunk per tileset, texels read with no filtering. Pass each tileset's atlas by name, as pixels, an `ImageBitmap`, a `GPUTexture` or a function.

```ts
import {EngineKernel} from 'margoengine/core';
import {createTileLayer, TileMap, type TileMapData} from 'margoengine/tilemap';
const canvas = document.querySelector('canvas')!;
const engine = await EngineKernel.create(canvas, {backend: 'webgpu', exactSize: [320, 180]});
const map: TileMapData = {
  width: 2, height: 1, tileWidth: 16, tileHeight: 16,
  layers: [createTileLayer('ground', 2, 1, Uint32Array.of(1, 2))],
  tilesets: [{name: 'grass', firstGid: 1, tileWidth: 16, tileHeight: 16, tileCount: 2, columns: 2}],
};
const image = await createImageBitmap(await (await fetch('grass.png')).blob());
const tiles = TileMap.attach(engine, {map, atlases: {grass: image}, camera: {x: 0, y: 0, zoom: 1}});
tiles.setTile('ground', 1, 0, 1); // only this cell's chunk goes up again
engine.render({delta: 1 / 60});
console.log(tiles.stats.draws); // 1
```

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `map` | required | The `TileMapData`. `setMap` swaps it |
| `atlases` | required | Tileset name to atlas. `setAtlas` swaps one |
| `camera` | `{x: 0, y: 0, zoom: 1}` | Map point at the top left and target pixels per map pixel, read each frame |
| `snap` | `true` | Rounds each layer's top left to a whole pixel, read each frame |
| `mapLayers` | every tile layer | Names of the tile layers to draw |
| `parallax` | `true` | Scrolls each layer by its own `parallax`; false when the camera carries it |
| `target` | the frame's colour target | Draw into this texture, or a function returning one |
| `clear` | the map's `backgroundColor`, else transparent | With `target`: colour to clear to, false draws over it |
| `order` | `10` | Frame-graph order |
| `layers` | `1` | Render-layer bits |
| `name` | `tilemap-1`, ... | Plugin name, unique per scene |

To draw into a compositor layer of `margoengine/pixel`, pass `target: layer.target, camera: layer.camera, parallax: false, mapLayers: ['ground']`, with one `TileMap` per layer that scrolls on its own.

Tiles animate by their `animation` steps on the `time` clock (milliseconds; each frame adds its delta), which changes a small lookup and no cells. A tile larger than the cell sits on the cell's bottom left, as in Tiled. Layer `offset`, `opacity`, `tint`, `visible` and `parallax` and tileset `margin`, `spacing` and `tileOffset` are honoured. Overlapping oversize tiles of different tilesets draw tileset by tileset. Object layers are data only: draw tile objects with `margoengine/sprites`. Image collection tilesets (`columns: 0`) must be packed into one atlas first. After writing into `layer.data` yourself, call `invalidate(layer)`.

## Isometric, staggered and hexagonal maps

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/tilemap.md]

=== @margoengine/vfx (packages/vfx/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/vfx

Import `margoengine/vfx` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/vfx` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

Optional GPU particle simulation and indirect billboard rendering, with capacity up to 1,000,000. One storage buffer holds particle position/life, velocity/size, color and rotation (birth angle, angular velocity, initial lifetime); each invocation owns one particle. Workgroups of 256 integrate gravity, analytic curl turbulence and ground-plane collisions, touching only position/life and velocity/size after birth. Births take the dead slots in slot order and the particles whose billboard can reach the screen are listed in slot order for the indirect draw, one triangle per particle (workgroup prefix sums, not atomic tickets), so the same frames give the same particles, the same draw order and the same blended pixels on every run.

```ts
import {EngineKernel} from 'margoengine/core';
import {VFX} from 'margoengine/vfx';
const engine = await EngineKernel.create(document.querySelector<HTMLCanvasElement>('#viewport')!, {backend:'webgpu'});
const sparks = VFX.attach(engine, {
  capacity:500_000, rate:20_000, position:[0,1,0], velocity:[0,5,0],
  spread:3, lifetime:[0.5,2], size:0.08, color:[1,0.4,0.05,1],
  gravity:[0,-9.81,0], ground:0, bounce:0.3, turbulence:1, angularVelocity:2
});
sparks.burst(10_000);
engine.start();
```

`rate` is births/second (default capacity/2). `burst(count)` adds births on the next frame, limited by capacity and available dead slots. Fractional emission budgets carry across frames. Options other than capacity can be adjusted before a frame; validation runs before GPU commands. `frequency` controls the curl field's spatial frequency. Life controls fade-out; rendering uses soft circular, camera-facing billboards with alpha blending and read-only scene depth. A billboard is never drawn under 1.5 px across: a smaller (far) particle is drawn at 1.5 px with its alpha scaled by its true area over that area, so it keeps its average light instead of flickering between pixels. Simulation starts with dead slots and performs no CPU particle initialization or GPU readback. `reset()` takes the effect back to that start: no particles, its clock at 0 and `initialCount` waiting, so the same frames after it give the same particles (`@margoengine/cutscene/vfx` seeks this way).

`emissionExtent: [x,y,z]` distributes births within a box of these half extents
around `position` (default zero). `intensity` multiplies RGB for HDR emission,
0..16 (default 1). Billboards draw at frame-graph order 6, after water and scatter.

One million particles use 64 MB for state plus 4 MB for the draw list, regardless of the live count. Per-frame CPU work is bounded uniform updates and pass submission; there is no JavaScript object/array per particle. GPU performance still depends on capacity, fill rate and hardware.

This is Margo's one particle system; `GPUParticles` in `@margoengine/creative/particles` is a leaf-field preset
over it. Six optional features patch the shaders only when set, so effects without them compile the same WGSL
and make the same GPU calls:

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/vfx.md]

=== @margoengine/creative (packages/creative/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/creative

Import `margoengine/creative` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/creative` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

WebGPU grass, a planet renderer, a leaf/weather particle preset, toon shading, HDR targets and a grading post effect (fog, god rays, focus blur, ACES, grain) for Margo Engine.

Each capability has one implementation: `GPUParticles` is a preset over `@margoengine/vfx`, bloom is `Bloom` from `@margoengine/post/bloom`, and sky backdrops are `Sky` from `@margoengine/sky`.

Package name: `@margoengine/creative`, version `1.0.0`. Build from source or install a local tarball until the renamed package is published.

```sh
npm install @margoengine/core@1.0.0 @margoengine/creative@1.0.0
```

```ts
import { Engine } from 'margoengine/core';
import { GPUParticles } from 'margoengine/creative/particles';

const canvas = document.querySelector<HTMLCanvasElement>('canvas')!;
const engine = await Engine.create(canvas, { backend: 'webgpu' });
GPUParticles.attach(engine, { count: 5000, sort: true, curl: 0.2 });
engine.start();
```

Call `engine.dispose()` on teardown. Creative rendering requires supported WebGPU hardware on HTTPS or localhost.

Use a feature subpath for a static import or an on-demand `import()`:

| Subpath | Feature |
| --- | --- |
| `@margoengine/creative/particles` | `GPUParticles` (a `@margoengine/vfx` preset) and particle option types |
| `@margoengine/creative/targets` | `HDRRenderTarget`, `TextureRenderTarget` |
| `@margoengine/creative/toon` | `ToonShading` and toon option types |
| `@margoengine/creative/paint` | `Painterly`: Kuwahara, watercolour wash and sketch, in an LDR PostStack |
| `@margoengine/creative/post` | `PostProcessing` (fog, god rays, focus blur, grading, grain) and its option types |
| `@margoengine/creative/grass` | `GrassField` and grass option types |
| `@margoengine/creative/planet` | `Planet` and planet option types |

```ts
const {Planet} = await import('margoengine/creative/planet'); // loaded only when this line runs
```

`GPUParticles({count, gravity, wind, size, curl, obstacles, sort, texture})` keeps `count` particles drifting
inside a 6 m cube centred on the origin, re-entering on the opposite face. It is a `VFX` from `@margoengine/vfx/base`
(`instanceof VFX` of that entry, with the obstacles, wrap, sort and texture features only; plugin name `gpu-particles`): `wind` is added to `gravity`, `curl` is VFX `turbulence`, and
`size` is the sprite half-width. Use `VFX` directly for emitters, lifetimes, bursts or up to 1,000,000 particles.

`PostProcessing` grades the HDR scene: exponential height fog, screen-space god rays, a depth-of-field focus
blur, exposure/contrast/saturation/gain/lift, ACES and grain. It has no bloom and no sky backdrop; passing
`bloom`, `threshold` or `atmosphere.sky`/`scattering`/`anisotropy` throws with the replacement. Alone it owns
scene capture. For bloom, or to combine it with SSAO, DOF or FXAA, add it to a `PostStack` from
`@margoengine/post/stack` as the display effect: `PostStack.attach(engine, [new SSAO(), new Bloom({strength:
0.3}), new PostProcessing({atmosphere: {density: 0.02}}), new FXAA()])`. In a stack its `target` is undefined.
For a sky behind the fog, attach `Sky` from `@margoengine/sky`.

Each subpath loads that feature and its dependencies. Existing named imports from `@margoengine/creative` remain available and can be tree-shaken by a bundler. `await import('@margoengine/creative')` loads the complete pack namespace; use a subpath when loading one feature independently. The stage's `addParticles` and `addEffects` (`@margoengine/stage/particles`, `/effects`) load only `/particles` and `/post`.

Attach a grass field directly to an existing Stage, without extending the facade:

```ts
import {createStage} from 'margoengine';
import {GrassField} from 'margoengine/creative/grass';

const stage = await createStage('#viewport', {backend: 'webgpu'});
const meadow = GrassField.attach(stage.engine, {
  blades: 100_000, area: [50, 50], bladeHeight: 1.2, windSpeed: 1.2, spores: true,
});
meadow.windStrength = 0.6;
// Remove this field early, or let stage.dispose() release it with the scene.
meadow.dispose();
```

`GrassField.attach(engine, options)` takes any core engine (`new GrassField({engine}, options)` is the older form). It advances `windTime` by the frame delta, supports multiple fields, and rebuilds GPU resources after device restoration. Do not add a second time increment in `onTick`. All roots lie on Y=0 in a rectangle centered on the origin.

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/creative.md]

=== @margoengine/procedural (packages/procedural/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/procedural

Import `margoengine/procedural` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/procedural` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

For minimum-spaced placement, import the optional [`/poisson` entry](#poisson-disk-placement).

`generateCabinMesh(height, position = [0,0])` builds a 6 × 8 m timber cabin,
35° roof, recessed windows/door and terrain-sunk stone/porch supports. `position`
is the world XZ origin used for terrain sampling. It returns `floor`, `siding`,
`roof`, `foundation` and `glass`; geometry remains local to that origin and floor.
Supply your own PBR materials and instance transform. Every terrain sample is
validated, and split architectural normals and UV-derived tangents are preserved.
Plank seams are closed, exterior window/door casings sit flush with the siding,
corner trim stands clear and overlapping roof courses have separate depth planes,
avoiding pinholes, fragmented thin edges and z-fighting. Solid gables meet the
siding faces and overlap the roof underside, closing the joint from elevated and
oblique views at both ends. Hidden
plank caps are omitted; trim closes the wall skin. Enterable cabin interiors would
need dedicated wall returns.
Porch post heights and the pitched crossbeam derive from the canopy underside,
keeping the supports below the roof while their bases follow terrain.

`createIslandHeight(seed = 731)` returns the coastal island preset's world-height
sampler. `generateGrassMesh(blades = 3)` returns crossed, tapered grass ribbons;
use 3/2/1 blades for scatter LODs with a double-sided material. Lower LODs remove
blades from the same ordered set, preserving the positions, normals, UVs and
tangents of surviving blades. Both are shared implementations used by the sandbox.

`createHumanoid(engine, [bodyMaterial, trimMaterial, visorMaterial])` creates a
jointed primitive rig and returns `root`, `focus`, `joints`, `knees` and `parts`.
Register `parts` with your shadow module. `poseHumanoid(rig, position, heading,
phase, speed)` writes a walk pose into the existing transforms in place.
The sandbox supplies phase/speed from the shared controls module.

`generateRockMesh()` produces deformed fieldstones with smooth, averaged normals
across split vertices while preserving UV seams and tangent frames.
`generateFernMesh()` produces seven curved, tapered ribbon fronds; use a
double-sided material. Both return `GeometryData` and are deterministic.
For the biome presets there are more plants: `generatePalmMesh()`, `generateBirchMesh()`, `generateAcaciaMesh()` and
`generateSnagMesh()` (a dead standing tree, empty canopy) return `{ trunk, canopy }` like `generateTreeMesh`, and
`generateCactusMesh()`, `generateReedMesh(stems = 9)` (double sided) and `generateTundraShrubMesh()` return one
`GeometryData`; each is rooted at the origin, +Y up, in metres.
Mesh levels for distance: `generateTreeMesh(kind, options)`, `generateShrubMesh`, `generateTundraShrubMesh`,
`generatePalmMesh`, `generateBirchMesh` and `generateAcaciaMesh` take `{ detail: 0 | 1 | 2 }` (default 2, the full
mesh, unchanged byte for byte). Level 1 keeps the shape with coarser lobes (a broadleaf canopy goes from 6,240 to
3,180 triangles); level 0 merges lobes into a few coarse ones for the far rings (400 triangles).
Level 1 keeps each axis of the canopy box within 20 percent of level 2; level 0 is stretched to level 2's box (conifer,
broadleaf, palm, birch, acacia and shrub canopies, within 10 percent on every axis), so far trees keep their size. An
invalid level throws a `RangeError`.

```ts
import {generateTreeMesh} from 'margoengine/procedural';
const rings = ([2, 1, 0] as const).map((detail) => generateTreeMesh('broadleaf', {detail})); // near, middle, far
```

For a cove scene there are two waterfront props, each one `GeometryData` mesh with UVs, tangents and unit normals,
local origin at the water surface (y = 0), +Y up, in metres, deterministic by `seed` (an integer, default 1):

| Call | Options (defaults) | Triangles at `detail` 2 / 1 / 0 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `generateJettyMesh(options?)` | `length` 4..120 (24), `width` 1..8 (2.2), `height` above the water 0.3..4 (1.1), `ladder` (true), `seed`, `detail` | 2,768 / 1,680 / 508 |
| `generateBoatMesh(options?)` | `length` 1.5..12 (3.6), `seats` 0..4 (3), `oars` (true), `seed`, `detail` | 1,884 / 812 / 372 |

The jetty runs along +X from the shore end at x = 0, with planks, stringers, posts and a ladder at the far end. The
boat is a rowing boat centred on the origin with its bow toward +X. A wrong type throws a `TypeError` and a value out of
range a `RangeError`; the message names the range to pass.

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/procedural.md]

=== @margoengine/wfc (packages/wfc/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/wfc

Import `margoengine/wfc` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/wfc` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

Seeded 3D Wave Function Collapse with weighted entropy, six-direction adjacency, pinned cells and bounded restart attempts.

```ts
import {WFC} from 'margoengine/wfc';
const generator = new WFC([4,4,4], [{neighbors: [[0],[0],[0],[0],[0],[0]]}]);
const cells = generator.solve(123);
```

Tile IDs are 0..31; output is a flattened Uint8Array with X fastest, then Y, then Z. Directions are +X, -X, +Y, -Y, +Z, -Z. Adjacency must be reciprocal. solve(seed, pins, attempts) retries contradictions deterministically and throws when the bounded budget is exhausted. This is local WFC propagation with restart, not an exhaustive backtracking solver or a guaranteed connected-dungeon generator; use the optional constraints entry for connected layouts, required paths and count limits. Tile weights must have finite sums and weighted logarithms; overflowing arithmetic is rejected.

## Overlapping model (`@margoengine/wfc/overlapping`, 2,457 B min+gzip)

Learns N x N patterns from a sample image and generates outputs in which every N x N window appears in the sample.

```ts
import {OverlappingModel} from 'margoengine/wfc/overlapping';
// 0 floor, 1 wall, 2 door; any numbers work (palette indices, packed RGBA).
const rows = ['11111111', '10000101', '10000201', '11211111', '10000001', '11111111'];
const model = new OverlappingModel({data: rows.join('').split('').map(Number), width: 8, height: 6}, {N: 3, symmetry: 8});
const image = model.solve(64, 40, {seed: 7, periodic: false});   // Float64Array of sample values, X fastest
console.log(model.patterns, model.stats.backtracks, model.stats.attempts);
```

Options: `N` 2..5, `periodicInput` (patterns wrap around the sample), `symmetry` 1..8 (rotations and reflections, in
Gumin's order); `solve` takes `seed`, `periodic` output, `backtracks` (per attempt, default 1000) and `attempts`
(default 4). Propagation is arc-consistent (supporter counts per cell, pattern and direction). On a contradiction the
latest choice is undone from the trail and forbidden in its cell (chronological backtracking); past the budget the
attempt restarts from scratch with the seed stream continuing; when the attempts run out `solve` throws. Every loop is
bounded by the budgets, so an unsatisfiable sample fails instead of hanging (the tests run one in a child process with a
timeout). A 7 x 7 maze sample with `symmetry: 1` fails every seed without backtracking and solves them all with it.
Limits: at most 4096 patterns, rejected during extraction before retaining a 4097th distinct pattern,
and `cells x patterns` <= 4,194,304 (memory: 18 bytes per cell and pattern); the
min-entropy scan is O(cells) per choice, fine to about 128 x 128; CPU only; works identically beside WebGPU and WebGL2 (tested in a real browser).
Example: `examples/overlapping.html`.

Apache-2.0. Optional, tree-shakable package; core peer: ^0.1.0 || ^1.0.0.

Build and unit tests: npm test --workspace @margoengine/wfc


## Fixed entrances and floors

Overlapping pins use output pixel coordinates and original sample values. Every covering pattern is restricted before
search, including the final N-1 pixels and periodic seams; backtracking cannot undo those restrictions.

```ts
import {OverlappingModel} from '@margoengine/wfc/overlapping';
const model = new OverlappingModel({data: [0,0,0,0], width: 2, height: 2}, {N: 2});
const image = model.solve(16, 12, {
  seed: 7,
  pins: [{position: [15, 0], value: 0}],
  ground: {value: 0, rows: 2},
});
console.log(image[15], image.at(-1));
```

Defaults: pins empty, ground absent, ground.rows 1, signal absent. Ground fixes the bottom image rows, and does not
forbid the value elsewhere. Pins and ground may coexist; conflicts or values absent from the sample exhaust the bounded
search and throw coded failed with a help link. Invalid coordinates/rows throw RangeError. A pre-aborted AbortSignal
throws its reason; synchronous checkpoints cannot receive new events while JavaScript owns the thread. No GPU resources
or shaders are used. Existing attempt/backtrack and memory limits apply. Generated binary/maze samples are stand-ins.
Heap/chunk backend selection and the paired Rust/Wasm SIMD measurement are documented below. Pattern extraction and the existing overlapping solver remain TypeScript.

## Global constraints (`@margoengine/wfc/constraints`, 2,484 B min+gzip)

=== @margoengine/splines (packages/splines/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/splines

Import `margoengine/splines` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/splines` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

Piecewise 3D Catmull-Rom, cubic Bezier, cubic Hermite, uniform B-spline and Kochanek-Bartels curves, with a cached arc-length lookup, closest point, stable frames, knot editing, mesh placement and bending, and curve fitting.

```ts
import {Spline} from 'margoengine/splines';
const curve = new Spline([[0,0,0], [5,1,5], [10,0,10]]);
const point = new Float64Array(3);
curve.atDistance(curve.length / 2, point);
curve.tangent(0.5, point);
```

Bezier curves require 3n+1 points and are open. Hermite requires one tangent per point; Catmull-Rom and Hermite can be closed. at uses t in 0..1; atDistance uses world units. Returned default output is reused, so provide an output buffer to retain multiple results. After editing points, call updateArcLengths. Arc lengths/tangents are numerical approximations controlled by divisions.

## More curve types

`kind: 'bspline'` is the uniform cubic B-spline: smoother than Catmull-Rom (continuous curvature) but it only pulls toward interior points, so it does not pass through them; open curves start and end exactly at the first and last point. `kind: 'kochanek-bartels'` passes through every point and adds `tension`, `continuity` and `bias`, each -1 to 1 and 0 by default (all zero is Catmull-Rom).

```ts
const waypoints: [number, number, number][] = [[0, 2, 0], [5, 3, 5], [10, 2, 10], [15, 4, 5]];
const camera = new Spline(waypoints, {kind: 'kochanek-bartels', tension: 0.3, bias: -0.2});
const smooth = new Spline(waypoints, {kind: 'bspline', closed: true});
```

## Closest point (`@margoengine/splines/closest`)

```ts
import {Spline} from 'margoengine/splines';
import {closestPointOnSpline} from 'margoengine/splines/closest';
const curve = new Spline([[0, 0, 0], [5, 1, 5], [10, 0, 10]]);
const hit = closestPointOnSpline(curve, [3, 1, 4]);
// hit.t (0..1), hit.arc (world units along the curve), hit.point, hit.distance
```

It samples the curve (`samples`, default the spline's `divisions`), then bisects on the slope of the distance around the best sample. A curve that passes close to itself (a tight spiral) needs `samples` high enough to tell the passes apart. `distanceAt(spline, t)` and `parameterAt(spline, distance)` convert between `t` and arc length.

## Stable frames and roll (`@margoengine/splines/frames`)

```ts
import {Spline} from 'margoengine/splines';
import {SplineFrames} from 'margoengine/splines/frames';
const curve = new Spline([[0, 0, 0], [5, 1, 5], [10, 0, 10]]);
const frames = new SplineFrames(curve, {up: [0, 1, 0], roll: (t) => t * 0.5});
const frame = frames.frameAt(curve.length * 0.25);
// frame.position, frame.tangent, frame.normal, frame.binormal (binormal = tangent x normal)
```

Frames are carried along the curve by double reflection (rotation-minimising), so they do not flip where a fixed up vector would (a curve passing through the up direction). `roll` is radians about the tangent: a function of `t`, or one value per knot (`knotCount(curve)`, blended linearly). A closed curve's twist is spread over its length so the last frame meets the first (`closeLoop: false` turns that off). Frames are sampled at `samples` (default 256) steps and blended in between.

## Knot editing (`@margoengine/splines/knots`)

```ts
import {KnotPath} from 'margoengine/splines/knots';
const path = new KnotPath([
  {position: [0, 0, 0], data: [1]},
  {position: [4, 3, 0], data: [2]},
  {position: [8, 0, 0], mode: 'linear', data: [4]},
]);
path.insertAt(0, 0.5);                 // split the first segment; the curve does not move
path.setMode(1, 'broken', {tangentOut: [0, 2, 0]});
const spline = path.toSpline();        // a Bezier Spline
const width = path.dataAt(0.7)[0];     // per-knot numbers blended along the curve
const [a, b] = path.split(2);          // two paths sharing knot 2
```

Modes: `auto` (smooth through the knot), `linear` (handles point at the neighbors; a segment between two linear knots is straight) and `broken` (the stored `tangentIn` and `tangentOut`, so a corner can point any way). `insertAt` keeps the shape by turning the new knot and its two neighbors `broken`; pass `false` as the third argument to insert an `auto` knot and let the curve reshape. A closed path builds an open Bezier whose last point is its first.

## Place and deform along a spline (`@margoengine/splines/mesh`)

=== @margoengine/animation (packages/animation/README.md) ===

# Margo Engine Animation

Import `margoengine/animation` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/animation` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

Optional WebGPU skeletal animation and morph targets, isolated from core and stage.

```ts
import {createStage} from 'margoengine';
import {loadGLTF} from 'margoengine/gltf-pro';
import {Animation} from 'margoengine/animation';
const stage = await createStage('#viewport', {backend:'webgpu',capacity:2048});
const model = await loadGLTF(stage.engine, '/RobotExpressive.glb');
const animation = Animation.attach(model);
animation.play('Walking');
animation.playing = false;
animation.seek(0.5);
animation.destroy();
model.destroy();
stage.dispose();
```

Parses glTF skins, joint hierarchies and inverse bind matrices. Samples STEP, LINEAR (quaternion slerp), and CUBICSPLINE tracks. Animation advances in seconds before the engine updates world matrices. A compute pass blends position/normal/tangent morphs before skinning and writes the vertex draw buffer. Bone matrices use read-only storage buffers, bounded by the GPU's storage limits rather than a fixed bone count.

Every skinned or morphed primitive of a device, across all its Animations, lives in a few shared storage buffers and deforms in one compute dispatch per buffer page and influence format (100 morphed models with two primitives each: one dispatch, not 200). Copies of one asset primitive (`cloneModel`) share one copy of its bind-pose vertices, morph deltas and skin influences; only the deformed output, weights and bones are per copy, and a copy's output starts as a GPU copy of the bind pose, so a hundred characters upload their vertices once. A primitive's deformed vertices start `primitive.deformedOffset` bytes (a multiple of 256) into `primitive.deformed`; gltf-pro, shadows, TAA, selection and picking read them there, and a custom reader binds or copies from that offset.

Use `animation.setMorph(nodeIndex, targetIndex, weight)` for manual expressions. Play a clip by name/index; set `loop:false` for one-shot playback. Up to eight influences per vertex are supported through paired `JOINTS_0`/`WEIGHTS_0` and optional `JOINTS_1`/`WEIGHTS_1`. Higher sets reject explicitly. No blending between clips is included.

Four-influence primitives keep their 32-byte influence records and the arithmetic of the per-primitive shader, bit for bit. An eight-influence primitive uses a 64-byte record and a second, lazily created compute pipeline; both formats can coexist in one model. Weights normalize across all present sets, including assets whose positive weights are entirely in the secondary set. Joint indices accept unsigned 8-bit or 16-bit accessors; weights accept Float32 or normalized unsigned 8-bit/16-bit accessors. Both sets require matching vertex counts, valid palette indices, nonnegative weights, and a positive combined sum.

Single-clip playback reuses sample buffers, quaternion arrays, palette matrices, and inverse-bind views. The animation hot path allocates no new typed arrays, quaternion copies, or GPU resources. Device restoration recreates both pipeline variants and the shared buffers. `sampleTrack()` retains its independently owned return value by default; an optional seventh `target: Float32Array` argument lets other consumers reuse their own output storage.

`createMaterialAnimation(model, {clip?, loop?})` plays a clip's `KHR_animation_pointer` STEP tracks on base-color `KHR_texture_transform` offset and scale (what `@margoengine/exporters` writes from `materialAnimations`): `seek(seconds)` writes the sampled UV transform into every primitive material of the targeted glTF material, and `dispose()` releases its claim on those properties. Given the opt-in `pointers` option, `Animation` also plays those channels, with every other `KHR_animation_pointer` channel it supports (see below); without it, it skips them and counts them in the clip's duration.

The separate `@margoengine/animator` package adds gameplay states, blend trees, additive masks and foot IK while reusing this pass's palette buffers. `sampleTrack()` is exported for animation consumers (matrix products: `@margoengine/math/mat4`).

Animation installs an optional `model.prepareDeformation` encoding hook. GPU
picking and explicit CPU snapshots use it to update the same skin/morph output
after a seek, bone edit or weight change without needing a beauty frame. Queries
do not advance playback time. The hook survives device restoration; disposal
removes only the animation instance's own hook. No CPU skinning copy is added to
the playback path.

Run the character demo at `/examples/robot-expressive.html` (also `character-animation.html`). RobotExpressive is by Tomás Laulhé with morphs by Don McCurdy (CC0). It is not a Khronos sample.

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/animation.md]

=== @margoengine/animator (packages/animator/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/animator

Import `margoengine/animator` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/animator` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

Optional gameplay animation on the existing `@margoengine/animation` skinning pass. Named states select clips, 1D trees interpolate neighboring samples, and 2D trees use normalized inverse-square distance weights with exact sample reproduction. State transitions crossfade a captured pose into the destination. Masked additive layers apply translation/scale/quaternion and morph deltas relative to a sampled reference pose. A zero reference scale component contributes an identity scale delta on that axis. Primitives sharing a node must have matching morph target counts, as required by glTF.

```ts
import {EngineKernel} from 'margoengine/core';
import {loadGLTF} from 'margoengine/gltf-pro';
import {Animation} from 'margoengine/animation';
import {Animator, addCCDChain, type CCDChain} from 'margoengine/animator';
const engine = await EngineKernel.create(document.querySelector<HTMLCanvasElement>('#viewport')!, {backend:'webgpu'});
const model = await loadGLTF(engine, '/hero.glb'); // clips named Idle, Walk, Run
const animation = Animation.attach(model);
const animator = Animator.attach(animation, {
  initial:'locomotion', parameters:{speed:0},
  states:{
    locomotion:{parameter:'speed', samples:[{value:0,clip:'Idle'},{value:1,clip:'Walk'},{value:3,clip:'Run'}]},
    idle:'Idle'
  },
  transitions:[{from:'locomotion',to:'idle',when:p=>p.speed<0,duration:0.15}]
});
animator.parameters.speed = 2;
engine.start();
```

For a 2D state use `{parameters:['strafe','forward'],samples:[{value:[0,0],clip:'Idle'},...]}` with unique coordinates. Parameters default to zero. 1D samples must be strictly increasing. Clips loop independently in seconds (`Animation.options.loop` false holds the last frame). `playing = false` pauses state time and crossfades; `Animation.options.speed` scales them, as for Animation playback. `transition(state,duration)` switches states explicitly; predicates are evaluated in declaration order, at most once per frame. Add a layer with `addLayer({clip:'Aim',weight:0.5,mask:[upperBodyNodeIndex,...]})`. Masks use glTF node indices. The returned function removes the layer; mutable weights are validated each frame. `referenceTime` defaults to zero.

`addFootIK({hip,knee,ankle,pole,raycast,offset,probeHeight})` requires a direct three-node leg chain. The callback receives a world-space origin above the current ankle and a downward ray. Return `{position,normal?}` or `null`; supply terrain collision data or an existing BVH. For a BVH raycast, adapt its result to `{position}` or `null`. Normals align the ankle's local +Y with the terrain. Bones/ancestors require positive scales. Unreachable targets clamp to the leg's reach; the pole chooses the knee bend direction. `solveTwoBoneIK()` is also exported as a standalone analytical solver.

## CCD chains (any length)

`addCCDChain(animator, chain)` adds a Cyclic Coordinate Descent IK chain (Wang and Chen 1991) for arms, spines, tails, tentacles or fingers, solved every frame after the pose, additive layers and foot IK. Each sweep goes from the last joint to the first; every joint turns, on its own, so the end effector moves toward the target, then its limit is applied. `joints` lists glTF node indices from the first joint to the last, each the child of the one before. The Animator keeps the chain object and reads `target`, `rotation`, `pole`, `weight` and the solve settings every frame, so move the target by writing into it:

```ts
const joint = (name: string) => model.asset.doc.nodes!.findIndex((node) => node.name === name);
const grab = () => console.log('reached');
const reach: CCDChain = {
  joints: [joint('Shoulder'), joint('Elbow'), joint('Wrist')], // glTF node indices
  target: [0.4, 1.3, 0.5],                   // world space; mutate it per frame
  rotation: null,                            // optional world rotation (x, y, z, w) for the last joint
  pole: [0.3, 1.0, -0.5],                    // optional: the elbow bends toward this point
  tip: [0, 0.08, 0],                         // optional effector offset in the last joint's space
  limits: [
    { type: 'cone', angle: 1.6, twist: [-0.5, 0.5] },        // shoulder: swing cone + twist range
    { type: 'hinge', axis: [1, 0, 0], min: -2.6, max: 0 },  // elbow: one axis, one range
    { type: 'euler', min: [-0.6, -0.3, -1], max: [0.6, 0.3, 1] }, // wrist: per-axis angles (XYZ)
  ],
  iterations: 16, tolerance: 0.001, weight: 1,
  onSolve: (result) => { if (result.reached) grab(); },
};
const remove = addCCDChain(animator, reach);
```

[README continues: https://margoengine.com/llms/packages/animator.md]

=== @margoengine/kinematics-constraints (packages/kinematics-constraints/README.md) ===

# @margoengine/kinematics-constraints

Import `margoengine/kinematics-constraints` from the `margoengine` package, or `@margoengine/kinematics-constraints` from this package alone; the two are the same module. Neither is on npm yet: the [Install](../../README.md#install) section lists the two routes that work today (run in a clone, or install local tarballs).

Standalone capsule, sphere and convex hull avoidance for IK targets and two-bone chains. The package projects targets out of proxy volumes, checks elbow and link clearance, and searches a shoulder swivel angle through a caller-supplied IK evaluator. It has no engine, renderer, physics, or Wasm dependency. ESM exports and declarations are tree-shakable; core, stage, animation, and the existing IK kernels remain unchanged.

Version `1.0.0` is source-only and has not been published to npm. From the repository root:

```sh
npm ci
npm run build --workspace @margoengine/kinematics-constraints
npm run test --workspace @margoengine/kinematics-constraints
npm pack --workspace @margoengine/kinematics-constraints --pack-destination test-results
```

Install the resulting tarball in another project with `npm install ./margoengine-kinematics-constraints-1.0.0.tgz`. No core peer dependency is required. The package is Apache-2.0 licensed.

## Interactive arm demo

From the repository root, run:

```sh
npm run modern:dev:extensions
```

Open [http://127.0.0.1:5173/examples/kinematics-constraints.html](http://127.0.0.1:5173/examples/kinematics-constraints.html). If Vite reports a different port, use that port with the same path. Drag the orange request across the torso, overhead, and across the waist. Switch from the capsule torso to a mixed scene with an additional sphere and capsule rail; every full-chain acceptance checks all active volumes.

The compact controls demonstrate full-chain `solve()` versus target-only `resolveTarget()`. Target-only mode hides the arm and explicitly certifies only the green target sphere. The full-chain readout separates the accepted physical gap, accepted pole angle, allowed `min(π, speed * dt)` pole window, actual accepted pole step, accepted hand displacement, and requested-target contact. Hand motion can be nonzero while the transported pole coordinate is unchanged; a held pose reports zero for both accepted displacements. Before solving, the demo conditions large requested translations toward a nominal 0.75 m/s using the configured damping response. This reduces large catch-up steps without rejecting a successful solve after its history has advanced; obstacle/reach projection can still alter displacement, so it is not a certified Cartesian or joint velocity limit. Raw requests outside the operational reach band remain diagnostic. A rejected conditioned request can advance through a smaller local step only if another complete `solve()` succeeds; otherwise the controller holds its last accepted pose. Exact angular overshoot is not exposed by the package and is not invented by the HUD.

Advanced settings expose the caller's live/fixed positive time step, angular search budget, required gap, and target damping time. Changing the scene, required gap, or damping constructs a new solver and starts from a newly validated initial pose; changing speed or search budget preserves solve history. Fixed time is per caller update and is not a display-frame-rate guarantee. The optional 25° shoulder/torso yaw assist is an application adapter, not a feature of the package: the rotationally symmetric torso capsule remains in the same frame while a proposed shoulder position and its complete link chain are checked before being committed together. Rejected shoulder candidates retain the accepted root and pose.

The [demo controller](../../examples/kinematics-constraints-controller.js) includes an analytical elbow callback with reused vector storage. It transports the last accepted bend reference between reach directions, so overhead and cross-body motion keep one continuous angle convention. Pointer rays meet a curved drag surface in front of the torso and waist. The demo renders analytical proxies directly, without character skinning, continuous collision detection, joint acceleration limits, or a physical safety guarantee. Reused buffers do not guarantee that the JavaScript runtime or renderer performs no allocations.


For a motion report, expand **Record a problem**, click **Start recording**, reproduce the issue, then click **Stop recording**. The stopped JSON is readable in the panel and can be downloaded explicitly. The temporary recorder keeps the latest 3,600 frame snapshots plus bounded control actions, including raw, paced and final retry targets, accepted and candidate poses, clearance, pole/hand steps, and caller settings. It stays disabled until started, stores only local in-memory numeric snapshots, and never uploads or saves automatically. Clear removes the captured trace from the panel.
